chapters.title: The Last Day
paragraphs: ECHECRATES: Phaedo, were you with Socrates in the prison yourself, on the day he drank the poison?
PHAEDO: Yes, Echecrates, I was.

ECHECRATES: I would very much like to hear about his death. What did he say in his last hours? We were told that he died by taking poison, but nobody could tell us anything more. No one from Phlius ever goes to Athens these days, and it has been a long time since any visitor from Athens came here, so we had no clear account.
PHAEDO: Did you not hear how the trial went?
ECHECRATES: Yes, someone told us about the trial. We could not understand why he was put to death long afterwards, and not at the time, since he had been condemned. What was the reason for that?
PHAEDO: It was a coincidence, Echecrates. The stern of the ship that the Athenians send to Delos had been crowned the day before his trial.
ECHECRATES: What ship is this?

PHAEDO: It is the ship in which, according to Athenian tradition, Theseus sailed to Crete, taking the fourteen young people with him, and saved them and himself. They are said to have vowed to Apollo then that, if they were saved, they would send a mission to Delos every year. The custom still continues. From the time the priest of Apollo crowns the stern of the ship until it has gone to Delos and come back, the whole voyage is a holy season, and the city may not be polluted by public executions during it. When contrary winds hold the vessel up, the trip there and back can take a very long time. As I was saying, the ship was crowned the day before the trial. That is why Socrates lay in prison for so long after he was condemned before he was put to death.
ECHECRATES: How did he die, Phaedo? What was said and done? And which of his friends were with him? Or did the authorities forbid them to be there, so that he died with no friends near him?
PHAEDO: No, several of them were with him.
ECHECRATES: If you have nothing else to do, I wish you would tell me what happened, as exactly as you can.

PHAEDO: I have nothing at all to do, and I will try to do what you ask. Being reminded of Socrates is always the greatest joy for me, whether I am speaking of him myself or hearing someone else speak of him.
ECHECRATES: You will have listeners who feel just as you do, and I hope you will be as exact as you can.

PHAEDO: I had a strange feeling in his company. I could hardly believe I was present at the death of a friend, and so I did not pity him, Echecrates. He died so fearlessly, and his words and manner were so noble and gracious, that he seemed to me blessed. I thought that he could not be going to the other world without a divine call, and that, if any man was ever happy when he got there, he would be. So I did not pity him, as might have seemed natural at such a moment. But I did not feel the pleasure I usually feel in philosophical discourse (for philosophy was what we were discussing). I was pleased, but there was a strange mixture of pain in the pleasure, because I kept thinking that he was soon to die. We all shared this double feeling. We were laughing and weeping by turns, especially the excitable Apollodorus — you know the sort of man?
ECHECRATES: Yes.
PHAEDO: He was quite beside himself, and I and all the rest of us were deeply moved.
ECHECRATES: Who was there?

PHAEDO: Of native Athenians, besides Apollodorus, there were Critobulus and his father Crito, Hermogenes, Epigenes, Aeschines and Antisthenes. Ctesippus of the deme of Paeania was there too, and Menexenus, and some others. Plato, if I am not mistaken, was ill.
ECHECRATES: Were there any foreigners?
PHAEDO: Yes: Simmias the Theban, Cebes, and Phaedondes, and Euclid and Terpison, who came from Megara.
ECHECRATES: And were Aristippus and Cleombrotus there?
PHAEDO: No, they were said to be in Aegina.
ECHECRATES: Was anyone else there?
PHAEDO: I think that these were nearly all.
ECHECRATES: Well, and what did you talk about?

PHAEDO: I will start at the beginning and try to repeat the whole conversation. On the days before, we had been in the habit of gathering early in the morning at the court where the trial took place, which is not far from the prison. We would wait there, talking with one another, until the doors opened (they did not open very early). Then we went in and usually spent the day with Socrates. On the last morning we gathered earlier than usual. The evening before, as we left the prison, we had heard that the sacred ship had come back from Delos, so we agreed to meet very early at the usual place. When we arrived, the jailer who answered the door did not let us in. He came out and told us to wait until he called us. 'For the Eleven,' he said, 'are with Socrates now. They are taking off his chains and giving orders that he is to die today.' He soon came back and said we could come in. When we went in, we found Socrates just freed from his chains, and Xanthippe, whom you know, sitting beside him with his child in her arms. When she saw us she cried out, as women will: 'O Socrates, this is the last time you will talk with your friends, or they with you.' Socrates turned to Crito and said: 'Crito, have someone take her home.' Some of Crito's people led her away, crying out and beating herself.

And when she had gone, Socrates sat up on the couch, bent his leg and rubbed it, and said as he rubbed: How strange a thing is what people call pleasure, and how curiously it is related to pain, which might be thought its opposite. The two are never present in a man at the same moment, and yet anyone who pursues one is usually forced to take the other; they are two bodies joined by a single head. And I cannot help thinking that, if Aesop had thought of them, he would have made a fable about God trying to end their quarrel and, when he could not, fastening their heads together. That is why, when one comes, the other follows. I know it from my own experience now: the pain in my leg, caused by the chain, seems to be followed by pleasure.

At this Cebes said: I am glad, Socrates, that you have mentioned Aesop. It reminds me of a question that many people have asked, and that Evenus the poet asked me only the day before yesterday. He is sure to ask it again, so if you would like me to have an answer ready for him, you may as well tell me what to say to him. He wanted to know why you, who never wrote a line of poetry before, are now in prison turning Aesop's fables into verse and also composing that hymn in honor of Apollo.

Tell him the truth, Cebes, he replied: that I had no idea of rivaling him or his poems, for I knew that would be no easy task. I wanted to see whether I could clear away a scruple I felt about the meaning of certain dreams. Throughout my life I have often had intimations in dreams 'that I should compose music.' The same dream came to me sometimes in one form and sometimes in another, but always with the same words, or nearly the same: 'Cultivate and make music,' said the dream. Until now I had supposed that it was only meant to urge and encourage me in the study of philosophy, which has been the pursuit of my life and is the noblest and best of music. The dream was telling me to do what I was already doing, just as the spectators tell a runner in a race to run when he is already running. But I was not certain of this, because the dream might have meant music in the popular sense of the word. I was under sentence of death, and the festival was giving me a respite, so I thought it would be safer to settle the scruple and, in obedience to the dream, compose a few verses before I departed.

First I made a hymn in honor of the god of the festival. Then I considered that a poet, if he is really to be a poet, should not only put words together but should invent stories, and I have no gift for invention. So I took some fables of Aesop, which I had at hand and knew (they were the first I came upon), and turned them into verse. Tell this to Evenus, Cebes, and tell him to be of good cheer. Say that I would have him come after me if he is a wise man, and not delay, and that I am likely to be going today, for the Athenians say that I must.
Simmias said: What a message for such a man! I have often kept his company, and as far as I know him, I should say he will never take your advice unless he is forced to.
Why, said Socrates, is Evenus not a philosopher?
I think he is, said Simmias.
Then he, or any man who has the spirit of philosophy, will be willing to die, but he will not take his own life, for that is held to be unlawful.
At this he changed his position, put his legs down from the couch to the ground, and stayed sitting for the rest of the conversation.
Why do you say, asked Cebes, that a man ought not to take his own life, but that the philosopher will be ready to follow the dying?
Socrates replied: Cebes and Simmias, you are disciples of Philolaus. Have you never heard him speak of this?
Yes, but what he said was obscure, Socrates.

My words too are only an echo, but there is no reason why I should not repeat what I have heard. Indeed, since I am going to another place, it is very fitting for me to think and talk about the nature of the journey I am about to make. What better use can I make of the time between now and sunset?

Then tell me, Socrates, why is suicide held to be unlawful? I have certainly heard Philolaus, whom you were just asking about, assert it when he was staying with us at Thebes, and others say the same too, although I have never understood what any of them meant.

Do not lose heart, replied Socrates, and the day may come when you will understand. I suppose you wonder why death alone is not allowed to be good for certain people at certain times, when other evil things may be good then. You wonder why, when a man is better off dead, he may not be his own benefactor, but must wait for someone else to do it.
Very true, said Cebes, laughing gently and speaking in his native Boeotian.

I admit that what I am saying looks inconsistent, but perhaps there is no real inconsistency after all. There is a doctrine, whispered in secret, that man is a prisoner who has no right to open the door and run away. This is a great mystery, which I do not quite understand. Yet I too believe that the gods are our guardians and that we are their possession. Do you not agree?
Yes, I quite agree, said Cebes.

Suppose one of your own possessions, an ox or an ass, for example, took it upon itself to put itself out of the way when you had given no sign that you wanted it to die. Would you not be angry with it, and would you not punish it if you could?
Certainly, replied Cebes.
Then, if we look at the matter this way, there may be some reason in saying that a man should wait, and should not take his own life until God summons him, as he is now summoning me.

Yes, Socrates, said Cebes, there seems to be truth in what you say. And yet how can you reconcile this seemingly true belief, that God is our guardian and we are his possessions, with the willingness to die that we just now attributed to the philosopher? It is not reasonable that the wisest of men should be willing to leave a service in which the gods, the best of rulers, rule over them. Surely no wise man thinks that when he is set free he can take better care of himself than the gods take of him. A fool may perhaps think so. He may argue that he had better run away from his master, without considering that his duty is to stay to the end and not to run away from what is good, and that there would be no sense in running away. The wise man will want always to be with one who is better than himself. Now this, Socrates, is the reverse of what was just said. On this view the wise man should be sorry to pass out of life, and the fool glad.
Socrates seemed pleased with Cebes' earnestness. Here, he said, turning to us, is a man who is always inquiring, and who is not convinced so easily by the first thing he hears.

And certainly, added Simmias, the objection he is making now does seem to me to have some force. What can it mean for a truly wise man to want to fly away and lightly leave a master who is better than himself? And I rather suspect that Cebes means you. He thinks you are too ready to leave us, and too ready to leave the gods, whom you admit to be our good masters.
Yes, replied Socrates, there is reason in what you say. And so you think I ought to answer your indictment as if I were in a court?
We would like you to, said Simmias.

Then I must try to defend myself more successfully before you than I did before the judges. For I am quite ready to admit, Simmias and Cebes, that I ought to be grieved at death if I were not persuaded of two things. The first is that I am going to other gods who are wise and good (of which I am as certain as I can be of any such matter). The second is that I am going (though I am less sure of this) to men who have departed and are better than those I leave behind. So I do not grieve as I might have done, for I have good hope that something remains for the dead and, as has been said of old, something far better for the good than for the evil.

But do you mean to take your thoughts away with you, Socrates? said Simmias. Will you not share them with us? They are a benefit in which we too have a right to share. Besides, if you succeed in convincing us, that will be an answer to the charge against you.
I will do my best, replied Socrates. But first you must let me hear what Crito wants. He has been wishing to say something to me for a long time.

Only this, Socrates, replied Crito: the attendant who is to give you the poison has been telling me, and he wants me to tell you, that you must not talk much. Talking, he says, raises the heat, and this tends to interfere with the action of the poison. People who get excited are sometimes forced to take a second or even a third dose.
Then, said Socrates, let him mind his own business and be ready to give the poison twice or even three times if necessary. That is all.
I knew quite well what you would say, replied Crito, but I had to satisfy him.
Never mind him, he said.

And now, O my judges, I want to prove to you that the real philosopher has reason to be of good cheer when he is about to die, and that after death he may hope to obtain the greatest good in the other world. How this can be, Simmias and Cebes, I will try to explain. I believe that the true follower of philosophy is likely to be misunderstood by other men. They do not see that he is always pursuing death and dying. If this is so, and he has desired death all his life, why should he complain when his time comes, about the very thing he has always pursued and desired?

Simmias said, laughing: Though I am not in a laughing mood, you have made me laugh, Socrates. For I cannot help thinking that, when the many hear your words, they will say how truly you have described philosophers. Our people at home will say the same, and add that the life philosophers desire is in fact death, and that they have found them out to be deserving of the death they desire.

chapters.title: The Philosopher and Death
paragraphs: And they are right, Simmias, to say so, except for the words 'they have found them out.' They have not found out what kind of death the true philosopher deserves, or how he deserves it or desires it. But enough about them. Let us discuss the matter among ourselves. Do we believe that there is such a thing as death?
To be sure, replied Simmias.

Is it not the separation of soul and body? And is being dead the completion of this, when the soul exists by itself, released from the body, and the body is released from the soul? What else is death but this?
Just so, he replied.

Here is another question, which will probably throw light on our inquiry if you and I can agree about it. Ought the philosopher to care about the pleasures of eating and drinking, if they are to be called pleasures?
Certainly not, answered Simmias.
And what about the pleasures of love? Should he care for them?
By no means.

And will he think much of the other ways of indulging the body, such as buying costly clothes, or sandals, or other adornments for the body? Does he not rather despise anything beyond what nature needs, instead of caring about it? What do you say?
I should say that the true philosopher would despise them.
Would you not say that he is entirely concerned with the soul and not with the body? As far as he can, he wants to get away from the body and turn to the soul.
Quite true.
In matters of this kind, then, philosophers more than all other men can be seen, in every way, to separate the soul from any association with the body.
Very true.

The rest of the world, Simmias, think that a man who finds no pleasure in such things and takes no part in bodily pleasures has a life not worth having, and that anyone who is indifferent to them is as good as dead.
That is also true.

What shall we say, then, about the actual acquiring of knowledge? If the body is invited to share in the inquiry, is it a hindrance or a help? I mean, is there any truth in sight and hearing? Are they not, as the poets are always telling us, inaccurate witnesses? And if even these are inaccurate and unclear, what is to be said of the other senses? For you will allow that they are the best of them?
Certainly, he replied.
Then when does the soul attain truth? For when it tries to examine anything in company with the body, it is obviously deceived.
True.
Then must true existence be revealed to it in thought, if it is revealed at all?
Yes.

And is thought best when the mind is gathered into itself and none of these things trouble it, neither sounds nor sights nor pain nor any pleasure, when it takes leave of the body and has as little to do with it as possible, with no bodily sense or desire, and is aspiring after true being?
Certainly.
And in this the philosopher dishonors the body, since his soul runs away from his body and desires to be alone and by itself?
That is true.
Well, here is another point, Simmias. Is there an absolute justice, or is there not?
Assuredly there is.
And an absolute beauty and an absolute good?
Of course.
But did you ever see any of them with your eyes?
Certainly not.

Or did you ever reach them with any other bodily sense? I speak not of these alone but of absolute greatness, and health, and strength, and of the essence or true nature of everything. Have you ever perceived the reality of any of them through the bodily organs? Or is it not rather the man who trains his intellectual vision to form the most exact conception of the essence of each thing he examines who comes nearest to knowing their several natures?
Certainly.

And the man who attains the purest knowledge of them is the one who goes to each with the mind alone. In the act of thought he does not bring in sight or any other sense along with reason. He uses the very light of the mind, in its own clearness, to search into the very truth of each thing. He has got rid, as far as he can, of eyes and ears and, so to speak, of the whole body, since in his opinion these are distracting elements that, when they infect the soul, hinder it from acquiring truth and knowledge. Who, if not he, is likely to attain the knowledge of true being?
What you say has a wonderful truth in it, Socrates, replied Simmias.

And when real philosophers consider all these things, will they not be led to a reflection that they will put into words something like this? 'Have we not found,' they will say, 'a path of thought that seems to bring us and our argument to this conclusion: as long as we are in the body, and the soul is infected with the evils of the body, our desire will not be satisfied? And our desire is for the truth. For the body is a source of endless trouble to us, simply because it needs food. It is also liable to diseases that overtake us and impede us in the search after true being. It fills us with loves and lusts and fears and fancies of all kinds and endless foolery, and in fact, as men say, takes away from us any power of thinking at all. Where do wars and fightings and factions come from? From nothing but the body and the lusts of the body. Wars are caused by the love of money, and money has to be acquired for the sake of the body and in its service. Because of all these obstacles we have no time for philosophy. And last and worst of all, even when we do have leisure and turn to some speculation, the body is always breaking in on us. It causes turmoil and confusion in our inquiries and so amazes us that it prevents us from seeing the truth.

Experience has shown us that if we want pure knowledge of anything, we must be rid of the body. The soul by itself must look at things in themselves. Then we shall attain the wisdom we desire, and of which we say we are lovers, not while we live but after death. For if the soul cannot have pure knowledge while in company with the body, one of two things follows: either knowledge cannot be attained at all, or it can be attained only after death. For then, and not before, the soul will be parted from the body and exist by itself alone. In this present life, I reckon, we come nearest to knowledge when we have as little dealing or association with the body as possible, and are not filled with its nature, but keep ourselves pure until the hour when God himself is pleased to release us. In this way, having got rid of the foolishness of the body, we shall be pure and have converse with the pure, and we shall know of ourselves the clear light everywhere, which is no other than the light of truth.' For the impure are not permitted to approach the pure. These are the kinds of words, Simmias, that the true lovers of knowledge cannot help saying to one another, and thinking. You would agree, would you not?
Undoubtedly, Socrates.

But, my friend, if this is true, there is great reason to hope that, going where I am going, I shall attain at the end of my journey what has been the pursuit of my life. And so I go on my way rejoicing, and not I only, but every other man who believes that his mind has been made ready and that he is in a manner purified.
Certainly, replied Simmias.

And what is purification but the separation of the soul from the body, as I was saying before? It is the habit of the soul to gather and collect itself into itself from every side out of the body, and to live in its own place alone, in this life as in another, as far as it can. It is the release of the soul from the chains of the body.
Very true, he said.
And this separation and release of the soul from the body is called death?
To be sure, he said.
And the true philosophers, and they alone, are always seeking to release the soul. Is not the separation and release of the soul from the body their special study?
That is true.
And, as I was saying at first, it would be a ridiculous contradiction for men to train themselves to live as near to a state of death as they can, and yet to complain when death comes upon them.
Clearly.

And the true philosophers, Simmias, are always busy practicing dying, and this is why death is less terrible to them than to any other men. Look at it this way. Suppose they have been enemies of the body in every way and want to be alone with the soul. When this desire of theirs is granted, how inconsistent they would be if they trembled and complained instead of rejoicing at departing for the place where they hope, when they arrive, to gain what they desired in life (and this was wisdom) and at the same time to be rid of the company of their enemy. Many a man has been willing to go to the world below, moved by the hope of seeing an earthly love, or wife, or son there, and talking with them. Will the man who is a true lover of wisdom, and is just as firmly persuaded that only in the world below can he enjoy her worthily, still complain at death? Will he not depart with joy? Surely he will, my friend, if he is a true philosopher. For he will be firmly convinced that only there, and nowhere else, can he find wisdom in her purity. And if this is true, he would be very absurd, as I was saying, to be afraid of death.
He would, indeed, replied Simmias.

And when you see a man complaining as death approaches, is not his reluctance proof enough that he is not a lover of wisdom but a lover of the body, and probably at the same time a lover of money or power, or both?
Quite so, he replied.
And is not courage, Simmias, a quality that especially marks the philosopher?
Certainly.

Then there is temperance, which even the common people take to consist in controlling and regulating the passions and in feeling superior to them. Is not temperance a virtue belonging only to those who despise the body and spend their lives in philosophy?
Most assuredly.
For if you consider the courage and temperance of other men, you will see that they are really a contradiction.
How so?
Well, he said, you know that men in general regard death as a great evil.
Very true, he said.
And do not courageous men face death because they fear yet greater evils?
That is quite true.
Then everyone except the philosophers is courageous only out of fear, because they are afraid. And yet it is surely strange that a man should be courageous from fear, because he is a coward.
Very true.

And are not the temperate in exactly the same case? They are temperate because they are intemperate. This might seem a contradiction, but it is nevertheless what happens with this foolish temperance. For there are pleasures they are afraid of losing, and in their desire to keep these they abstain from some pleasures because they are overcome by others. Men call being conquered by pleasure intemperance, yet to these people conquering pleasure consists in being conquered by pleasure. That is what I mean by saying that in a sense they are made temperate through intemperance.
That appears to be the case.

Yet the exchange of one fear or pleasure or pain for another fear or pleasure or pain, and of the greater for the less, as if they were coins, is not an exchange of virtue. My blessed Simmias, is there not one true coin for which all things ought to be exchanged? That coin is wisdom. Only in exchange for this, and in company with this, is anything truly bought or sold, whether courage or temperance or justice. Is not all true virtue the companion of wisdom, no matter what fears or pleasures or other similar goods or evils may or may not accompany it? But the virtue that is made up of these goods, when they are cut off from wisdom and exchanged with one another, is only a shadow of virtue. There is no freedom or health or truth in it. In the true exchange, however, all these things are purged away, and temperance and justice and courage and wisdom herself are the purgation. The founders of the mysteries seem to have had a real meaning, and were not talking nonsense, when they hinted in a figure long ago that whoever passes unsanctified and uninitiated into the world below will lie in a slough, but whoever arrives there after initiation and purification will dwell with the gods.

For 'many,' as they say in the mysteries, 'are the thyrsus-bearers, but few are the mystics,' meaning, as I interpret the words, 'the true philosophers.' During my whole life I have been seeking, as well as I could, to find a place among them. Whether I have sought in a right way or not, and whether I have succeeded or not, I shall truly know in a little while, if God will, when I myself arrive in the other world. That is my belief. And so I maintain that I am right, Simmias and Cebes, in not grieving or complaining at parting from you and my masters in this world, for I believe that I shall find good masters and friends in another world just as much. But most men do not believe this. If, then, my defense convinces you better than it did the Athenian judges, it will be well.

Cebes answered: I agree, Socrates, with the greater part of what you say. But when it comes to the soul, men tend to be incredulous. They fear that when it has left the body its place may be nowhere, and that on the very day of death it may perish and come to an end. As soon as it is released from the body, they think, it will go forth scattered like smoke or air, and in its flight vanish into nothingness. If only it could be gathered into itself after it has obtained release from the evils you speak of, there would be good reason to hope, Socrates, that what you say is true. But surely it takes a great deal of argument and many proofs to show that when a man is dead his soul still exists and has any force or intelligence.
True, Cebes, said Socrates. Shall I suggest that we talk a little about the probabilities of these things?
I am sure, said Cebes, that I should greatly like to know your opinion about them.

I reckon, said Socrates, that no one who heard me now, not even one of my old enemies, the Comic poets, could accuse me of idle talk about matters that are none of my concern. If you please, then, let us go on with the inquiry.

chapters.title: The Argument from Opposites
paragraphs: Let us look at the question whether the souls of men are in the world below after death, or are not. An ancient doctrine comes to my mind. It says that souls go from here to the other world, and that they come back here and are born again from the dead. Now if the living really do come from the dead, then our souls must exist in the other world, for otherwise how could they be born again? This would be conclusive if we had real evidence that the living are born only from the dead. If we do not, then we shall have to bring other arguments.
Very true, replied Cebes.

Then let us not limit the question to man. Let us take animals in general, and plants, and everything that has generation, and the proof will be easier. Are not all things that have opposites generated out of their opposites? I mean things like good and evil, or just and unjust — and there are countless other opposites that are generated out of opposites. What I want to show is that in all opposites there is, of necessity, a similar alternation. I mean, for example, that anything which becomes greater must have been less before it became greater.
True.
And whatever becomes less must once have been greater, and then have become less.
Yes.
And the weaker comes into being from the stronger, and the swifter from the slower.
Very true.
And the worse comes from the better, and the more just from the more unjust.
Of course.
And does this hold for all opposites? Are we convinced that every one of them is generated out of its opposite?
Yes.

And in this universal opposition of all things, are there not also two intermediate processes that are always going on, from one opposite to the other and back again? Where there is a greater and a less, there is also an intermediate process of increase and diminution. What grows is said to wax, and what decays is said to wane.
Yes, he said.

And there are many other processes, such as division and composition, or cooling and heating, which equally involve a passage into and out of one another. This holds of all opposites necessarily, even though it is not always expressed in words. They are really generated out of one another, and there is a passing, or process, from each to the other?
Very true, he replied.
Well, is there not an opposite of life, as sleep is the opposite of waking?
True, he said.
And what is it?
Death, he answered.
And if these are opposites, are they generated the one from the other, and do they have their two intermediate processes as well?
Of course.

Now, said Socrates, I will analyze one of the two pairs of opposites I have mentioned, together with its intermediate processes, and you shall analyze the other for me. I call one pair sleep and waking. The state of sleep is opposed to the state of waking. Out of sleeping, waking is generated, and out of waking, sleeping. The process of generation in the one case is falling asleep, and in the other waking up. Do you agree?
I entirely agree.
Then analyze life and death for me in the same way. Is not death opposed to life?
Yes.
And are they generated one from the other?
Yes.
What is generated from the living?
The dead.
And what from the dead?
I can only answer — the living.
Then the living, whether things or persons, Cebes, are generated out of the dead?
That is clear, he replied.
Then we must infer that our souls exist in the world below?
That is true.
And one of the two processes, or generations, is visible — for surely the act of dying is visible?
Surely, he said.
What then are we to conclude? Shall we leave out the opposite process? Shall we suppose that nature walks on one leg only? Or must we not assign to death some corresponding process of generation?
Certainly, he replied.
And what is that process?
Return to life.
And return to life, if there is such a thing, is the birth of the dead into the world of the living?
Quite true.

Then here is a new way of reaching the conclusion that the living come from the dead, just as the dead come from the living. If this is true, it gives us a most certain proof that the souls of the dead exist in some place, and that they come back again from there.
Yes, Socrates, he said; the conclusion seems to follow necessarily from what we have already admitted.

And these admissions were not unfair, Cebes, he said. I think we can show that as follows. Suppose generation went in a straight line only, with no compensation or circle in nature, and no turn or return of elements into their opposites. Then, as you know, all things would at last take on the same form and pass into the same state, and there would be no more generation of them.
What do you mean? he said.

It is a simple thing, which I will illustrate by the case of sleep, he replied. You know that if sleeping and waking did not alternate, the story of the sleeping Endymion would in the end have no meaning, because everything else would be asleep too, and he would be no different from the rest. Or suppose there were only composition and no division of substances: then the chaos of Anaxagoras would come again. And in the same way, my dear Cebes, suppose everything that partook of life were to die, and after dying stayed in the form of death and did not come to life again. Then everything would at last be dead and nothing would be alive — what other result could there be? For if the living spring from anything other than the dead, and those living things die too, must not everything at last be swallowed up in death? (But compare Republic.)
There is no escape, Socrates, said Cebes; and your argument seems to me absolutely true.

Yes, he said, Cebes, in my opinion it is and must be so. We have not been deluded in making these admissions. I am confident that there truly is such a thing as living again, that the living spring from the dead, that the souls of the dead are in existence, and that the good souls have a better portion than the evil.

chapters.title: The Argument from Recollection
paragraphs: Cebes added: Your favorite doctrine, Socrates, is that knowledge is simply recollection. If that is true, it also necessarily implies that at some earlier time we learned what we now recollect. That would be impossible unless our soul had existed somewhere before it took the form of man. So here is another proof that the soul is immortal.
But tell me, Cebes, said Simmias, interrupting, what arguments are offered in favor of this doctrine of recollection? I am not very sure at the moment that I remember them.

One excellent proof, said Cebes, comes from questions. If you put a question to someone in the right way, he will give a true answer of his own accord. But how could he do that unless knowledge and right reason were already in him? This is shown most clearly when he is taken to a diagram or anything of that sort. (Compare Meno.)

But if you are still unconvinced, Simmias, said Socrates, I would ask whether you might agree with me if you look at the matter in another way — I mean, if you still doubt whether knowledge is recollection.

I am not unconvinced, said Simmias; but I want this doctrine of recollection to be brought back to my own recollection. From what Cebes has said, I am beginning to recollect and to be convinced. Still, I should like to hear what you were going to say.
This is what I would say, he replied: We should agree, if I am not mistaken, that whatever a man recollects, he must have known at some earlier time.
Very true.

And what is the nature of this knowledge, or recollection? Let me put it this way. Suppose a person sees or hears or in some other way perceives something. He knows that thing, but he also has a conception of something else, which is the object of a different kind of knowledge, not the same one. May we not fairly say that he recollects the thing of which he has the conception?
What do you mean?
I mean what I can illustrate by the following example: The knowledge of a lyre is not the same as the knowledge of a man?
True.

And yet think of what lovers feel when they recognize a lyre, or a garment, or anything else their beloved has been in the habit of using. Knowing the lyre, do they not form in the mind's eye an image of the youth to whom the lyre belongs? That is recollection. In the same way anyone who sees Simmias may remember Cebes; and there are endless examples of the same thing.
Endless, indeed, replied Simmias.
And recollection is most commonly a process of recovering what has already been forgotten through time and inattention.
Very true, he said.
Well, and may you not also, from seeing the picture of a horse or a lyre, remember a man? And from the picture of Simmias, may you not be led to remember Cebes?
True.
Or you may even be led to the recollection of Simmias himself?
Quite so.
And in all these cases, the recollection may come from things that are either like or unlike?
It may.
And when the recollection comes from like things, another question is sure to arise: does the likeness fall short, in any degree, of the thing recollected, or not?
Very true, he said.

chapters.title: The Affinity Argument
paragraphs: And shall we go a step further and affirm that there is such a thing as equality — not the equality of one piece of wood or stone with another, but something over and above this, absolute equality? Shall we say so?
Say so, yes, replied Simmias, and swear to it, with all the confidence in the world.
And do we know the nature of this absolute essence?
To be sure, he said.

And where did we get our knowledge of it? Did we not see equalities among material things, such as pieces of wood and stones, and gather from them the idea of an equality that is different from them? For you will admit that it is different. Or look at the matter another way: do not the same pieces of wood or stone appear equal at one time and unequal at another?
That is certain.
But are real equals ever unequal? Or is the idea of equality the same as the idea of inequality?
Impossible, Socrates.
Then these so-called equals are not the same as the idea of equality?
Clearly not, I should say, Socrates.
And yet it was from these equals, though they differ from the idea of equality, that you conceived and reached that idea?
Very true, he said.
Whether it is like them, or unlike them?
Yes.
But that makes no difference. Whenever the sight of one thing made you conceive another, whether like or unlike, there must surely have been an act of recollection?
Very true.

But what would you say of equal pieces of wood and stone, or other material equals? What impression do they make on us? Are they equal in the same sense in which absolute equality is equal? Or do they fall short of that perfect equality to some degree?
Yes, he said, and to a very great degree.

And must we not allow this: when I, or anyone, looks at an object and observes that the thing he sees aims at being some other thing but falls short of it and cannot be that other thing, being inferior, then whoever makes this observation must have had previous knowledge of the thing which the other resembles but falls short of?
Certainly.
And has not this been our own case with equals and absolute equality?
Precisely.
Then we must have known equality before the time when we first saw material equals and reflected that all these apparent equals strive to reach absolute equality but fall short of it?
Very true.
And we recognize also that this absolute equality has been known only through sight or touch or some other of the senses, and can be known only through them, since they are all alike in this respect?
Yes, Socrates, as far as the argument is concerned, one of them is the same as another.
So it is from the senses that we learn that all sensible things aim at an absolute equality which they fall short of?
Yes.

Then before we began to see or hear or perceive in any way, we must already have had knowledge of absolute equality. Otherwise we could not have referred the equals we get from the senses to that standard — for they all aspire to it, and all fall short of it.
No other inference can be drawn from what has been said.
And did we not see and hear and use our other senses as soon as we were born?
Certainly.
Then we must have acquired the knowledge of equality at some earlier time?
Yes.
That is to say, before we were born, I suppose?
True.

And if we acquired this knowledge before we were born, and were born having the use of it, then before birth and at the moment of birth we knew not only the equal, the greater and the less, but all the other ideas as well. For we are speaking not only of equality but of beauty, goodness, justice, holiness, and of everything to which we give the name of essence in the dialectical process, both when we ask questions and when we answer them. Of all this we may certainly affirm that we acquired the knowledge before birth?
We may.

But suppose that, having acquired this knowledge, we have not forgotten what we acquired in each case. Then we must always have come into life with knowledge, and we shall go on knowing as long as life lasts — for to know is to acquire knowledge, keep it, and not lose it. Is not forgetting, Simmias, just the losing of knowledge?
Quite true, Socrates.

But suppose the knowledge we acquired before birth was lost by us at birth, and that afterwards, by using the senses, we recovered what we had known before. Will not the process we call learning be the recovery of knowledge that is natural to us? And may this not rightly be called recollection?
Very true.

So much is clear: when we perceive something by sight, or hearing, or some other sense, that perception enables us to form a notion of some other thing, like or unlike, that is associated with it but has been forgotten. Hence, as I was saying, one of two alternatives follows. Either we had this knowledge at birth and continued to know all through life; or, after birth, those who are said to learn are only remembering, and learning is simply recollection.
Yes, that is quite true, Socrates.
And which alternative do you prefer, Simmias? Did we have the knowledge at our birth, or did we recollect afterwards the things we had known before our birth?
I cannot decide at the moment.
At any rate you can decide this: will a person who has knowledge be able to give an account of it, or not? What do you say?
Certainly, he will.
But do you think that every man is able to give an account of the very matters we are speaking about?
I wish they could, Socrates, but I rather fear that by this time tomorrow there will no longer be anyone alive who can give an account of them as it ought to be given.
Then you do not think, Simmias, that all men know these things?
Certainly not.
They are in the process of recollecting what they learned before?
Certainly.
But when did our souls acquire this knowledge? Not since we were born as men?
Certainly not.
And therefore earlier?
Yes.
Then, Simmias, our souls must also have existed without bodies before they took the form of man, and must have had intelligence.
Unless, Socrates, you suppose that these notions are given us at the very moment of birth; for that is the only time left.
Yes, my friend, but if so, when do we lose them? For they are not in us when we are born — that is admitted. Do we lose them at the moment of receiving them? Or if not, at what other time?
No, Socrates, I see that I was talking nonsense without realizing it.

Then may we not say, Simmias, that if, as we are always repeating, there is an absolute beauty, and goodness, and an absolute essence of all things; and if we refer all our sensations to this, which is now discovered to have existed in our former state, and compare them with it, finding these ideas to be pre-existent and our inborn possession, then our souls must have had a prior existence; but if not, there would be no force in the argument? The proof that these ideas existed before we were born is the same as the proof that our souls existed before we were born; and if the ideas did not, then neither did the souls.

Yes, Socrates; I am convinced that the necessity is exactly the same for the one as for the other. The argument retreats successfully to the position that the existence of the soul before birth cannot be separated from the existence of the essence you speak of. For nothing seems to me so evident as that beauty, goodness, and the other notions you were just mentioning have a most real and absolute existence; and I am satisfied with the proof.
Well, but is Cebes equally satisfied? For I must convince him too.

I think, said Simmias, that Cebes is satisfied. He is the most incredulous of mortals, yet I believe he is sufficiently convinced that the soul existed before birth. But that the soul will go on existing after death is not yet proven, even to my own satisfaction. I cannot get rid of the feeling of the many, which Cebes was referring to — the feeling that when a man dies the soul will be dispersed, and that this may be the end of it. For grant that it may have been born elsewhere, put together out of other elements, and in existence before it entered the human body. Why, after it has entered in and gone out again, may it not itself be destroyed and come to an end?

Very true, Simmias, said Cebes; about half of what was required has been proven, namely that our souls existed before we were born. That the soul will exist after death as well as before birth is the other half, for which the proof is still missing and has to be supplied. When that is given, the demonstration will be complete.

But that proof, Simmias and Cebes, has already been given, said Socrates, if you put the two arguments together — I mean this one and the former one, in which we admitted that everything living is born of the dead. For if the soul exists before birth, and when it comes to life and is born it can be born only from death and dying, must it not continue to exist after death, since it has to be born again? Surely the proof you want has already been furnished. Still, I suspect that you and Simmias would be glad to probe the argument further. Like children, you are haunted by a fear that when the soul leaves the body, the wind may really blow it away and scatter it, especially if a man happens to die in a great storm and not when the sky is calm.

Cebes answered with a smile: Then, Socrates, you must argue us out of our fears — and yet, strictly speaking, they are not our fears. There is a child within us to whom death is a sort of hobgoblin; him too we must persuade not to be afraid when he is alone in the dark.
Socrates said: Let the voice of the charmer be applied every day, until you have charmed the fear away.
And where shall we find a good charmer for our fears, Socrates, when you are gone?

Hellas, he replied, is a large place, Cebes, and has many good men; and there are not a few barbarian races. Seek him among them all, far and wide, sparing neither pains nor money, for there is no better way to spend your money. And you must seek among yourselves too, for you will not find others better able to make the search.
The search, replied Cebes, shall certainly be made. And now, if you please, let us return to the point in the argument where we digressed.
By all means, replied Socrates; what else should I please?
Very good.

Must we not, said Socrates, ask ourselves what it is that we imagine to be liable to being scattered, and for which we fear? And what, again, is it for which we have no fear? Then we can go on to inquire whether what suffers dispersion is of the nature of soul or not. Our hopes and fears about our own souls will turn on the answers to these questions.
Very true, he said.

Now the compound, or composite, may be supposed to be naturally capable of being dissolved, just as it is capable of being compounded. But the uncompounded, and only that, must be indissoluble, if anything is.
Yes, I should imagine so, said Cebes.
And the uncompounded may be assumed to be always the same and unchanging, whereas the compound is always changing and never the same.
I agree, he said.

Then now let us return to the previous discussion. Take that idea or essence which in the dialectical process we define as essence or true existence — the essence of equality, of beauty, or of anything else. Are these essences liable at times to some degree of change? Or is each of them always what it is, having the same simple, self-existent and unchanging form, and not admitting of variation at all, or in any way, or at any time?
They must be always the same, Socrates, replied Cebes.

And what would you say of the many beautiful things — men or horses or garments or anything else that goes by the same names and may be called equal or beautiful? Are they all unchanging and always the same, or quite the reverse? May they not rather be described as almost always changing, and hardly ever the same, either with themselves or with one another?
The latter, replied Cebes; they are constantly changing.
And these you can touch and see and perceive with the senses, but the unchanging things you can perceive only with the mind — they are invisible and cannot be seen?
That is very true, he said.
Well then, added Socrates, let us suppose that there are two sorts of existence — one seen, the other unseen.
Let us suppose them.
The seen is the changing, and the unseen is the unchanging?
That may be supposed too.
And further, is not one part of us body, and another part soul?
To be sure.
And to which class is the body more alike and more closely akin?
Clearly to the seen — no one can doubt that.
And is the soul seen or not seen?
Not by man, Socrates.
And by 'seen' and 'not seen' we mean what is or is not visible to the eye of man?
Yes, to the eye of man.
And is the soul seen or not seen?
Not seen.
Unseen, then?
Yes.
Then the soul is more like the unseen, and the body more like the seen?
That follows necessarily, Socrates.

And were we not saying long ago that when the soul uses the body as an instrument of perception — that is, when it uses sight or hearing or some other sense (for perceiving through the body means perceiving through the senses) — the soul is then dragged by the body into the region of the changeable? Were we not saying that it wanders and is confused, that the world spins around it, and that it is like a drunkard when it touches change?
Very true.

But when the soul returns into itself and reflects, it passes into the other world, the region of purity, and eternity, and immortality, and unchangeableness, which are its kindred. It lives with them always when it is by itself and is not hindered. Then it ceases from its erring ways, and being in communion with the unchanging, it is itself unchanging. And this state of the soul is called wisdom?
That is well and truly said, Socrates, he replied.
And to which class is the soul more nearly alike and akin, as far as we can infer from this argument and from the preceding one?
I think, Socrates, that everyone who follows the argument will say that the soul is infinitely more like the unchangeable — even the most stupid person will not deny that.
And the body is more like the changing?
Yes.

Yet consider the matter once more in another light. When soul and body are united, nature orders the soul to rule and govern, and the body to obey and serve. Now which of these two functions is akin to the divine, and which to the mortal? Does not the divine appear to you to be what naturally orders and rules, and the mortal to be what is subject and serves?
True.
And which does the soul resemble?
The soul resembles the divine, and the body the mortal — there can be no doubt of that, Socrates.

Then reflect, Cebes. Is not this the conclusion from all that has been said: that the soul is in the very likeness of the divine, and immortal, and intellectual, and uniform, and indissoluble, and unchangeable; and that the body is in the very likeness of the human, and mortal, and unintellectual, and multiform, and dissoluble, and changeable? Can this, my dear Cebes, be denied?
It cannot.
But if it is true, is not the body liable to quick dissolution, and is not the soul almost or altogether indissoluble?
Certainly.

And do you also observe this? After a man is dead, the body, the visible part of him, lies in the visible world and is called a corpse. It would naturally be dissolved and decomposed and dissipated, yet it is not dissolved or decomposed at once. It may remain for some time, even a long time, if the constitution was sound at the time of death and the season of the year is favorable. For a body that has shrunk and been embalmed, as is done in Egypt, may remain almost whole through countless ages; and even when a body decays, some parts of it, such as the bones and ligaments, are practically indestructible. Do you agree?
Yes.

And is it likely, then, that the soul, which is invisible, will be blown away and destroyed immediately on leaving the body, as the many say? The soul is passing to a place like itself, the place of the true Hades, which is invisible, and pure, and noble. It is on its way to the good and wise God, where, if God will, my own soul is soon to go. If this is the soul's nature and origin, can that be? Never, my dear Simmias and Cebes. The truth is rather this. Suppose the soul is pure at departing and draws after it no bodily taint, because it never willingly had anything to do with the body during life, but always avoided it and gathered itself into itself — making this separation its constant study, which means that it has been a true disciple of philosophy and has in fact always been practicing dying. For is not philosophy the practice of death? —
Certainly —

That soul, I say, itself invisible, departs to the invisible world, to the divine and immortal and rational. Arriving there, it is secure of bliss and is released from the error and folly of men, from their fears and wild passions and all other human ills, and dwells forever, as they say of the initiated, in company with the gods (compare Apol.). Is not this true, Cebes?
Yes, said Cebes, beyond a doubt.

But take the soul that has been polluted and is impure at the time of its departure. It has been the companion and servant of the body always, in love with the body and fascinated by it, and by its desires and pleasures, until it comes to believe that truth exists only in bodily form, which a man may touch and see and taste and use for his lusts. Such a soul is accustomed to hate and fear and avoid the intellectual principle, which to the bodily eye is dark and invisible and can be attained only by philosophy. Do you suppose that such a soul will depart pure and unalloyed?
Impossible, he replied.
It is held fast by the corporeal, which the continual association and constant care of the body have worked into its nature.
Very true.

And this corporeal element, my friend, is heavy and weighty and earthy. It is the element of sight, by which a soul is weighed down and dragged back into the visible world, because it is afraid of the invisible and of the world below. It prowls about tombs and sepulchres, near which, as they tell us, ghostly apparitions of souls are seen — souls that have not departed pure, but are cloyed with sight and therefore visible.
(Compare Milton, Comus:

'But when lust, By unchaste looks, loose gestures, and foul talk, But most by lewd and lavish act of sin, Lets in defilement to the inward parts, The soul grows clotted by contagion, Imbodies, and imbrutes, till she quite lose, The divine property of her first being. Such are those thick and gloomy shadows damp Oft seen in charnel vaults and sepulchres, Lingering, and sitting by a new made grave, As loath to leave the body that it lov'd, And linked itself by carnal sensuality To a degenerate and degraded state.')
That is very likely, Socrates.

Yes, that is very likely, Cebes; and these must be the souls not of the good but of the evil, which are compelled to wander about such places as payment of the penalty for their former evil way of life. They continue to wander until, through the craving for the corporeal which never leaves them, they are finally imprisoned in another body. And we may suppose that they find their prisons in the same natures they had in their former lives.
What natures do you mean, Socrates?
I mean that men who have given themselves to gluttony, wantonness and drunkenness, with no thought of avoiding them, would pass into asses and animals of that sort. What do you think?
I think such an opinion is exceedingly probable.
And those who have chosen the portion of injustice, and tyranny, and violence will pass into wolves, or into hawks and kites — where else can we suppose them to go?
Yes, said Cebes; with such natures, beyond question.
And there is no difficulty, he said, in assigning each of them a place answering to its nature and propensities?
There is not, he said.

Some are happier than others. The happiest, both in themselves and in the place they go to, are those who have practiced the civil and social virtues called temperance and justice, which are acquired by habit and attention without philosophy and mind. (Compare Republic.)
Why are they the happiest?

Because they may be expected to pass into some gentle and social kind like their own, such as bees or wasps or ants, or back again into the form of man; and just and moderate men may be supposed to spring from them.
Very likely.

No one who has not studied philosophy, and who is not entirely pure at the time of his departure, is allowed to enter the company of the Gods; only the lover of knowledge may. And this is the reason, Simmias and Cebes, why the true votaries of philosophy abstain from all fleshly lusts, and hold out against them and refuse to give themselves up to them. They do this not because they fear poverty or the ruin of their families, like the lovers of money and the world in general; nor, like the lovers of power and honor, because they dread the dishonor or disgrace of evil deeds.
No, Socrates, that would not become them, said Cebes.

No indeed, he replied; and therefore those who care about their own souls, and do not merely live molding and fashioning the body, say farewell to all this. They will not walk in the ways of the blind. When philosophy offers them purification and release from evil, they feel that they ought not to resist her influence, and they turn and follow wherever she leads.
What do you mean, Socrates?

I will tell you, he said. The lovers of knowledge are aware that the soul was simply fastened and glued to the body. Until philosophy received it, it could view real existence only through the bars of a prison, not in and through itself. It was wallowing in the mire of every sort of ignorance, and because of lust it had become the principal accomplice in its own captivity. This was its original state. Then, as I was saying, and as the lovers of knowledge are well aware, philosophy saw how terrible its confinement was, and that the soul was itself the cause of it. Philosophy received the soul and gently comforted it, and sought to release it. She pointed out that the eye and the ear and the other senses are full of deception. She persuaded the soul to withdraw from them, to abstain from all but their necessary use, and to be gathered up and collected into itself. She bade it trust in itself and in its own pure apprehension of pure existence, and mistrust whatever comes to it through other channels and is subject to variation; for such things are visible and tangible, but what the soul sees in its own nature is intelligible and invisible.

And the soul of the true philosopher thinks that it ought not to resist this deliverance, and therefore abstains from pleasures and desires and pains and fears as far as it can. It reflects that when a man has great joys or sorrows or fears or desires, he suffers from them not merely the sort of evil that might be expected — for example, the loss of his health or property, which he has sacrificed to his lusts — but an evil far greater, which is the greatest and worst of all evils, and one he never thinks of.
What is it, Socrates? said Cebes.

The evil is this: when the feeling of pleasure or pain is most intense, every soul of man imagines that the objects of this intense feeling are then plainest and truest. But this is not so; they are really the things of sight.
Very true.
And is it not in this state that the soul is most enslaved by the body?
How so?

Why, because each pleasure and pain is a sort of nail which nails and rivets the soul to the body, until it becomes like the body and believes that to be true which the body affirms to be true. Since it agrees with the body and has the same delights, it is obliged to have the same habits and haunts. It is not likely ever to be pure when it departs to the world below, but is always infected by the body. So it sinks into another body and there germinates and grows, and therefore has no part in the communion of the divine and pure and simple.
Most true, Socrates, answered Cebes.
This, Cebes, is why the true lovers of knowledge are temperate and brave, and not for the reason most people give.
Certainly not.

Certainly not! The soul of a philosopher reasons in quite a different way. It will not ask philosophy to release it only to hand itself over again, once released, to the bondage of pleasures and pains. That would be doing a job only to have it undone, weaving instead of unweaving a Penelope's web. Instead, the soul calms the passions and follows reason. It stays in the contemplation of reason, looking at what is true and divine (which is not a matter of opinion), and it draws its nourishment from that. So it seeks to live in this way while it lives, and after death it hopes to go to what is its own kin and like itself, and to be free of human ills. Never fear, Simmias and Cebes, that a soul nurtured like this, with these pursuits, will be scattered and blown away by the winds when it leaves the body, and be nowhere and nothing.

When Socrates had finished speaking, there was silence for a long time. He seemed to be thinking over what had been said, and so were most of us. Only Cebes and Simmias were talking a little with one another. Socrates noticed them and asked what they thought of the argument, and whether anything was missing from it. For, he said, there are many points still open to suspicion and attack, if anyone wants to examine the matter thoroughly. If you are considering some other subject, I will say no more. But if you are still in doubt, do not hesitate to say exactly what you think. Tell us if you can suggest anything better, and if you think I can be of any use, let me help you.

Simmias said: I must confess, Socrates, that we did have doubts. Each of us kept urging the other to ask the question we wanted answered, and neither of us liked to ask it. We feared that our insistence might be a trouble to you at a time like this.

Socrates replied with a smile: Simmias, what are you saying? I am not likely to persuade other men that I do not regard my present situation as a misfortune, if I cannot even persuade you that I am no worse off now than at any other time in my life. Will you not grant that I have as much of the gift of prophecy as the swans? When swans sense that they must die, they sing more strongly than ever, after singing all their lives. They rejoice that they are about to go to the god whose servants they are. But men are afraid of death themselves, and so they slanderously claim that the swans sing a lament at the end. They do not consider that no bird sings when it is cold, or hungry, or in pain, not even the nightingale, the swallow or the hoopoe, which are said to sing a song of sorrow. I do not believe that of them any more than of the swans. Because the swans are sacred to Apollo, they have the gift of prophecy. They foresee the good things of the other world, and that is why they sing and rejoice on that day more than ever before. And I too believe that I am the consecrated servant of the same god, and a fellow-servant of the swans. I think I have received from my master a gift of prophecy no less than theirs, and so I would not go out of life any less cheerfully than the swans.
So never mind, if that is your only objection. Speak and ask whatever you like, while the eleven magistrates of Athens allow it.

Very well, Socrates, said Simmias. Then I will tell you my difficulty, and Cebes will tell you his. I feel (and I daresay you feel it too) how hard, or rather impossible, it is to reach any certainty about such questions in this present life. And yet I would think him a coward who did not test what is said about them to the utmost, or who gave up before he had examined them from every side. He should persevere until he has done one of two things. Either he should discover the truth about them, or be taught it. Or, if that is impossible, he should take the best and most unanswerable of human theories and let it be the raft on which he sails through life. I admit this is not without risk, if he cannot find some word of God that will carry him more surely and safely. And now, as you bid me, I will venture to question you, and then I will not have to reproach myself later for not saying at the time what I think. When I consider the matter, either alone or with Cebes, the argument certainly does seem to me, Socrates, to be insufficient.
Socrates answered: I dare say, my friend, that you may be right. But I should like to know in what respect the argument is insufficient.

chapters.title: The Objections
paragraphs: In this respect, replied Simmias. Suppose someone used the same argument about harmony and the lyre. Might he not say that harmony is invisible, incorporeal, perfect and divine, and exists in the lyre that is harmonized, while the lyre and the strings are matter, material, composite, earthy, and akin to what is mortal? Then someone breaks the lyre, or cuts and tears the strings. The man who takes this view would argue as you do, on the same analogy, that the harmony survives and has not perished. You cannot imagine, he would say, that the lyre without its strings, and the broken strings themselves, which are mortal, remain, while the harmony, which is of heavenly and immortal nature and kin, has perished, and perished before the mortal thing. The harmony must still be somewhere, he would say, and the wood and the strings will decay before anything can happen to it. This thought, Socrates, must have occurred to you too, since this is just our own conception of the soul. The body is, so to speak, strung and held together by the elements of hot and cold, wet and dry, and the soul is the harmony, the due and proportionate mixture of them. But if so, then whenever the strings of the body are loosened or overstrained beyond measure by disease or some other injury, the soul must perish at once, though it is most divine, just like other harmonies, whether of music or of works of art. Meanwhile the material remains of the body may last a considerable time, until they decay or are burned.
And if someone maintains that the soul, being the harmony of the elements of the body, is the first thing to perish in what is called death, how shall we answer him?

Socrates looked steadily at us, as was his way, and said with a smile: Simmias has reason on his side. And why does not one of you who is better able than I am answer him? There is force in his attack on me. But perhaps, before we answer him, we had better hear what Cebes has to say too, so that we gain time to think. When both have spoken, we can either agree with them, if there is truth in what they say, or, if not, hold our position. Please tell me then, Cebes, he said, what was the difficulty that troubled you?

chapters.title: The Final Argument
paragraphs: Cebes said: I will tell you. My feeling is that the argument stands where it did, and is open to the same objections as before. I am ready to admit that the existence of the soul before it entered the bodily form has been proven very ingeniously and, if I may say so, quite sufficiently. But its existence after death is still, in my judgment, unproven. My objection is not the same as Simmias'. I am not inclined to deny that the soul is stronger and longer-lasting than the body, since I think the soul far excels the body in all such respects. Well then, the argument says to me, why are you still unconvinced? When you see that the weaker thing continues to exist after the man is dead, will you not admit that the longer-lasting thing must also survive for the same length of time? Now I ask you to consider whether my objection, which like Simmias I will put in a figure, carries any weight. My analogy is that of an old weaver who dies. After his death somebody says: He is not dead, he must be alive. See, there is the coat he wove and wore himself, and it remains whole and undecayed. Then he asks someone who does not believe him whether a man lasts longer, or a coat that is in use and being worn. When he is told that a man lasts far longer, he thinks he has proven beyond doubt that the man survives, because the longer-lasting thing is safe if the shorter-lasting thing remains.

But that, Simmias, as I beg you to notice, is a mistake. Anyone can see that a man who talks like this is talking nonsense. The truth is that the weaver, having woven and worn many such coats, outlived several of them and was outlived only by the last. That does not prove a man to be slighter and weaker than a coat. The relation of the body to the soul can be expressed in a similar figure. Anyone could fairly say in the same way that the soul is long-lasting and the body weak and short-lived by comparison. He could argue in the same way that every soul wears out many bodies, especially if a man lives many years. While he is alive, the body wastes and decays, and the soul keeps weaving a new garment and repairing the loss. But whenever the soul perishes, of course it must be wearing its last garment, and that garment will outlast it. Then, once the soul is dead, the body will at last show its native weakness, and quickly decompose and pass away. So I would rather not rely on the argument from superior strength to prove that the soul continues to exist after death.

Suppose I grant even more than you say is possible. Suppose I acknowledge not only that the soul existed before birth, but also that the souls of some exist and will continue to exist after death, and will be born and die again and again, and that the soul has a natural strength that will hold out through many births. Even so, we may still be inclined to think that it will grow weary in the labors of successive births, and may at last give way in one of its deaths and perish utterly. This death and dissolution of the body, which brings destruction to the soul, may be unknown to any of us, since none of us can have had any experience of it. If so, then I maintain that anyone who is confident about death has a foolish confidence, unless he can prove that the soul is altogether immortal and imperishable. If he cannot prove the soul's immortality, then a man who is about to die will always have reason to fear that, when the body is separated from it, the soul may also perish utterly.

All of us, as we told one another afterwards, felt uneasy at hearing what they said. We had been so firmly convinced before. Now to have our faith shaken seemed to bring confusion and uncertainty, not only into the earlier argument, but into any future one. Either we were incapable of forming a judgment, or there were no grounds for belief.

ECHECRATES: There I feel with you, by heaven I do, Phaedo. While you were speaking, I began to ask myself the same question: what argument can I ever trust again? What could be more convincing than the argument of Socrates, which has now fallen into discredit? The doctrine that the soul is a harmony has always had a wonderful attraction for me. When it was mentioned, it came back to me at once, as my own original conviction. And now I must begin again and find another argument that will assure me that when a man is dead, his soul survives. Tell me, I implore you, how did Socrates go on? Did he seem to share the uneasiness you mention? Or did he meet the attack calmly? And did he answer forcefully or feebly? Tell me what happened as exactly as you can.

PHAEDO: Often, Echecrates, I have wondered at Socrates, but never more than on that occasion. That he was able to answer was nothing. What astonished me was, first, the gentle, pleasant and approving way in which he received the words of the young men. Then there was how quickly he felt the wound the argument had inflicted, and how readily he healed it. He could be compared to a general rallying his defeated and broken army, urging them to follow him and return to the field of argument.
ECHECRATES: What followed?

PHAEDO: You shall hear. I was close to him on his right hand, seated on a sort of stool, and he was on a couch that was a good deal higher. He stroked my head and pressed the hair down on my neck (he had a way of playing with my hair), and then he said: Tomorrow, Phaedo, I suppose these fair locks of yours will be cut off.
Yes, Socrates, I suppose they will, I replied.
Not if you take my advice.
What shall I do with them? I said.

Today, he replied, and not tomorrow, if this argument dies and we cannot bring it back to life, you and I will both shave our locks. And if I were you, and the argument got away from me and I could not hold my ground against Simmias and Cebes, I would take an oath myself, like the Argives, not to wear my hair long again until I had renewed the fight and defeated them.
Yes, I said, but even Heracles is said to be no match for two.
Then summon me, he said, and I will be your Iolaus until the sun goes down.
I summon you, I replied, but not as Heracles summoning Iolaus. Rather as Iolaus might summon Heracles.
That will do as well, he said. But first let us take care to avoid a danger.
What kind of danger? I said.

That we become misologists, he replied. No worse thing can happen to a man than this. For just as there are misanthropists, or haters of men, there are also misologists, or haters of ideas, and both spring from the same cause, which is ignorance of the world. Misanthropy comes from too much confidence born of inexperience. You trust a man and think him altogether true, sound and faithful, and then in a little while he turns out to be false and a knave. Then it happens with another, and another. When this has happened several times to a man, especially among those he took to be his own most trusted and familiar friends, and he has often quarreled with them, he ends by hating all men and believing that no one has any good in him at all. You must have noticed this trait of character?
I have.

And is that feeling not discreditable? Is it not obvious that such a man, in dealing with other men, clearly had no experience of human nature? For experience would have taught him the true state of things: that the good are few and the evil are few, and that the great majority are somewhere in between.
What do you mean? I said.

I mean, he replied, what you might say of the very large and the very small. Nothing is more uncommon than a very large or a very small man. This applies generally to all extremes, whether of great and small, swift and slow, fair and foul, or black and white. And whether the examples you pick are men or dogs or anything else, the extremes are few and the cases in between are many. Have you never noticed this?
Yes, I said, I have.
And do you not imagine, he said, that if there were a competition in evil, the worst would turn out to be very few?
Yes, that is very likely, I said.

Yes, that is very likely, he replied. In this respect, though, arguments are unlike men. There you led me on to say more than I had intended. The point of the comparison was this. A simple man with no skill in dialectics believes an argument to be true, and afterwards imagines it to be false, whether it really is or not. Then it happens with another argument, and another, and he has no faith left. And great disputers, as you know, come in the end to think they have become the wisest of mankind, because they alone see the utter unsoundness and instability of all arguments, or indeed of all things, which, like the currents in the Euripus, go up and down in a never-ceasing ebb and flow.
That is quite true, I said.

Yes, Phaedo, he replied, and how melancholy it is, if there is such a thing as truth, or certainty, or the possibility of knowledge, that a man should have hit upon some argument that at first seemed true and then turned out to be false. Instead of blaming himself and his own lack of wit, he is annoyed, and ends by being only too glad to shift the blame from himself to arguments in general. Then for ever afterwards he hates and reviles them, and loses truth and the knowledge of realities.
Yes, indeed, I said; that is very melancholy.

Let us then, in the first place, he said, be careful not to allow into our souls the notion that there is no health or soundness in any arguments at all. Let us say rather that we have not yet reached soundness in ourselves, and that we must struggle manfully and do our best to gain health of mind. You and all other men must do this with your whole future life in view, and I myself with death in prospect. At this moment I am aware that I do not have the temper of a philosopher. Like the vulgar, I am only a partisan. When a partisan is engaged in a dispute, he cares nothing about the rights of the question and is anxious only to convince his hearers of his own assertions. The only difference between him and me at present is this. He seeks to convince his hearers that what he says is true, while I am rather seeking to convince myself, and convincing my hearers is a secondary matter for me. And see how much I gain by the argument. If what I say is true, then I do well to be persuaded of the truth. But if there is nothing after death, still, during the short time that remains, I shall not distress my friends with lamentations, and my ignorance will not last but will die with me, and so no harm will be done. This is the state of mind, Simmias and Cebes, in which I approach the argument.

And I ask you to think of the truth and not of Socrates. Agree with me if I seem to you to be speaking the truth. If not, oppose me with all your might, so that in my enthusiasm I do not deceive you as well as myself, and like the bee leave my sting in you before I die.

And now let us go on, he said. First let me be sure that I have in mind what you were saying.
