Simmias, if I remember rightly, fears and doubts whether the soul, although a fairer and more divine thing than the body, may not perish first, since it is in the form of harmony. Cebes, on the other hand, seemed to grant that the soul was longer-lasting than the body. But he said that no one could know whether the soul, after wearing out many bodies, might not perish itself and leave its last body behind. And this, he said, is death: the destruction not of the body but of the soul, since in the body the work of destruction is always going on. Are these not the points we have to consider, Simmias and Cebes?
They both agreed to this statement of them.
He went on: And did you deny the force of the whole preceding argument, or of only a part?
Of only a part, they replied.

And what did you think, he said, of the part in which we said that knowledge was recollection, and inferred from this that the soul must have existed somewhere else before it was enclosed in the body?

Cebes said that he had been wonderfully impressed by that part of the argument, and that his conviction remained absolutely unshaken. Simmias agreed, and added that he could hardly imagine ever thinking differently.

But, Socrates rejoined, you will have to think differently, my Theban friend, if you still maintain that harmony is a compound, and that the soul is a harmony made out of strings set in the frame of the body. For surely you will never allow yourself to say that a harmony exists before the elements that compose it.
Never, Socrates.

But do you not see that this is what you imply when you say that the soul existed before it took the form and body of man, and that it was made up of elements that did not yet exist? Harmony is not like the soul, as you suppose. First the lyre, the strings and the sounds exist in a state of discord, and then harmony is made last of all, and perishes first. How can such a notion of the soul agree with the other?
Not at all, replied Simmias.
And yet, he said, there surely ought to be harmony in a discourse whose subject is harmony.
There ought, replied Simmias.
But there is no harmony, he said, between the two propositions that knowledge is recollection and that the soul is a harmony. Which of them will you keep?

I think, he replied, that I have much stronger faith, Socrates, in the first of the two, which has been fully demonstrated to me, than in the second, which has not been demonstrated at all but rests only on probable and plausible grounds, and is therefore believed by the many. I know too well that arguments from probabilities are impostors. Unless great caution is used with them, they are apt to deceive, in geometry and in other things too. But the doctrine of knowledge and recollection has been proven to me on trustworthy grounds. The proof was that the soul must have existed before it came into the body, because the essence, whose very name implies existence, belongs to it. I am convinced that I have accepted this conclusion rightly and on sufficient grounds. So I must, I suppose, stop arguing, and stop allowing others to argue, that the soul is a harmony.
Let me put the matter, Simmias, he said, from another point of view. Do you imagine that a harmony, or any other composition, can be in a state other than that of the elements it is compounded from?
Certainly not.
Or do or suffer anything other than they do or suffer?
He agreed.
Then a harmony does not, properly speaking, lead the parts or elements that make it up, but only follows them.
He assented.
For a harmony cannot possibly have any motion, or sound, or other quality that is opposed to its parts.
That would be impossible, he replied.
And does not the nature of every harmony depend on the manner in which the elements are harmonized?
I do not understand you, he said.

I mean that a harmony admits of degrees. It is more of a harmony, and more completely a harmony, when it is more truly and fully harmonized, to whatever extent is possible. And it is less of a harmony, and less completely a harmony, when it is less truly and fully harmonized.
True.
But does the soul admit of degrees? Is one soul in the very least degree more or less a soul, or more or less completely a soul, than another?
Not in the least.
Yet surely of two souls, one is said to have intelligence and virtue and to be good, and the other to have folly and vice and to be an evil soul. And is this said truly?
Yes, truly.

But what will those who maintain that the soul is a harmony say about this presence of virtue and vice in the soul? Will they say that here is another harmony and another discord? Will they say that the virtuous soul is harmonized and, being itself a harmony, has another harmony within it, while the vicious soul is not harmonized and has no harmony within it?
I cannot tell, replied Simmias, but I suppose that those who say the soul is a harmony would assert something of the sort.

And we have already admitted that no soul is more a soul than another. That is equivalent to admitting that one harmony is not more or less a harmony, or more or less completely a harmony, than another?
Quite true.
And whatever is no more and no less a harmony is no more and no less harmonized?
True.
And whatever is no more and no less harmonized cannot have more or less harmony, only an equal harmony?
Yes, an equal harmony.
Then, since one soul is not more or less absolutely a soul than another, it is not more or less harmonized?
Exactly.
And therefore it has neither more nor less of discord, nor of harmony?
It has not.
And having neither more nor less of harmony or of discord, one soul has no more vice or virtue than another, if vice is discord and virtue harmony?
Not at all more.
Or to speak more correctly, Simmias, the soul, if it is a harmony, will never have any vice, because a harmony, being absolutely a harmony, has no part in what is not harmonical.
No.
And therefore a soul that is absolutely a soul has no vice?
How can it have, if the previous argument holds?
Then, if all souls are equally souls by their nature, all the souls of all living creatures will be equally good?
I agree with you, Socrates, he said.
Do you think all this can be true? he said. For these are the consequences that seem to follow from assuming that the soul is a harmony.
It cannot be true.
Once more, he said: is there any ruler of the elements of human nature other than the soul, and especially the wise soul? Do you know of one?
No, I do not.

And does the soul agree with the affections of the body, or does it oppose them? For example, when the body is hot and thirsty, does the soul not pull us against drinking? And when the body is hungry, against eating? This is only one instance out of ten thousand of the soul opposing the things of the body.
Very true.

But we have already acknowledged that the soul, being a harmony, can never sound a note against the tensions, relaxations, vibrations and other affections of the strings that compose it; it can only follow them and cannot lead them?
It must be so, he replied.

And yet do we not now find the soul doing the exact opposite? It leads the elements it is believed to be composed of. Almost always, throughout life, it opposes and coerces them in all sorts of ways. Sometimes it does so more violently, with the pains of medicine and gymnastics; sometimes more gently. Now it threatens the desires, passions and fears, and now it warns them, as if talking to something that is not itself. Homer in the Odyssey shows Odysseus doing this in the words —
'He beat his breast, and thus reproached his heart: Endure, my heart; far worse hast thou endured!'

Do you think Homer wrote this believing that the soul is a harmony that the affections of the body can lead? Or did he think it a nature that should lead and master them — itself a far diviner thing than any harmony?
Yes, Socrates, I quite think so.
Then, my friend, we can never be right to say that the soul is a harmony. We would contradict the divine Homer, and we would contradict ourselves.
True, he said.
So much, said Socrates, for Harmonia, your Theban goddess, who has graciously yielded to us. But what shall I say, Cebes, to her husband Cadmus, and how shall I make peace with him?

I think you will find a way to win him over, said Cebes. I am sure you have handled the argument with Harmonia in a way I never expected. When Simmias was explaining his difficulty, I quite imagined that no answer could be given to him. So I was surprised to find that his argument could not withstand the first onset of yours, and it is not impossible that the other, whom you call Cadmus, may meet a similar fate.

Nay, my good friend, said Socrates, let us not boast, in case some evil eye drives off the word I am about to speak. That we may leave in the hands of those above. I will draw near in Homeric fashion and test the mettle of your words. Here is the point. You want it proven to you that the soul is imperishable and immortal. You think the philosopher who is confident in death has a vain and foolish confidence, if he believes he will fare better in the world below than a man who has led another sort of life — unless he can prove this. And you say that showing the soul to be strong and divine, and to have existed before we became men, does not necessarily imply that it is immortal. Grant that the soul is long-lived, and that it knew and did much in a former state. It is still not immortal on that account. Its entrance into the human form may be a sort of disease, the beginning of its dissolution, and after the toils of life it may at last end in what is called death. And, as you say, it makes no difference to the fears of individuals whether the soul enters the body once or many times. For any man who is not devoid of sense must fear, if he has no knowledge and can give no account of the soul's immortality.
This, or something like it, I suspect to be your notion, Cebes. I come back to it on purpose, so that nothing escapes us, and so that you may add or take away anything, if you wish.
But, said Cebes, as far as I can see at present, I have nothing to add or take away. You have said what I mean.

Socrates paused for a while and seemed to be absorbed in thought. At length he said: You are raising a tremendous question, Cebes, which involves the whole nature of generation and corruption. If you like, I will tell you my own experience of it. If anything I say can help toward solving your difficulty, you may make use of it.
Cebes said: I would very much like to hear what you have to say.

Then I will tell you, said Socrates. When I was young, Cebes, I had a prodigious desire to know that department of philosophy called the investigation of nature. It seemed to me a lofty calling to know the causes of things, and why each thing comes to be, is destroyed, and is. I was always agitating myself with questions like these. Is the growth of animals the result of some decay that the hot and the cold contract, as some have said? Is the blood what we think with, or the air, or the fire? Or perhaps none of these — perhaps the brain is the origin of the perceptions of hearing, sight and smell, and memory and opinion come from them, and science rests on memory and opinion once they have become fixed. Then I went on to examine how these things are corrupted, and then the things of heaven and earth. In the end I concluded that I was utterly and absolutely unfit for these inquiries, as I will prove to you to your satisfaction.

For I was so fascinated by them that my eyes went blind to things I had seemed to myself, and to others, to know quite well. I forgot what I had earlier thought self-evident truths, for example that a man grows as a result of eating and drinking. When food is digested, flesh is added to flesh and bone to bone, and whenever congenial elements are gathered together, the smaller bulk becomes larger and the small man becomes great. Was that not a reasonable notion?
Yes, said Cebes, I think so.

Well, let me tell you something more. There was a time when I thought I understood the meaning of greater and less pretty well. When I saw a big man standing by a small one, I fancied that one was taller than the other by a head. Or one horse would appear to be greater than another horse. And still more clearly did I seem to perceive that ten is two more than eight, and that two cubits are more than one, because two is the double of one.
And what is your notion of such matters now? said Cebes.

I am far from imagining, he replied, that I know the cause of any of them, by heaven I am. For I cannot satisfy myself that when one is added to one, the one to which the addition is made becomes two, or that the two units added together make two by reason of the addition. I cannot understand how each of them was one and not two when it was separate from the other, and yet now that they are brought together, their mere juxtaposition or meeting should be the cause of their becoming two. Nor can I understand how dividing one is the way to make two. For then a different cause would produce the same effect. In the former instance the addition and juxtaposition of one to one was the cause of two; in this one, the separation and subtraction of one from the other would be the cause. Nor am I any longer satisfied that I understand why one, or anything else, is generated or destroyed or is at all. But I have in mind some confused notion of a new method, and I can never admit the other.

Then I heard someone reading, as he said, from a book of Anaxagoras, that mind was the disposer and cause of all. I was delighted with this notion, which seemed to me quite admirable, and I said to myself: If mind is the disposer, mind will dispose all for the best and put each particular in the best place. I argued that anyone who wanted to find the cause of the generation, destruction or existence of anything must find out what state of being, doing or suffering was best for that thing. So a man had only to consider what is best for himself and for others, and then he would also know what is worse, since the same science comprehends both. I rejoiced to think that I had found in Anaxagoras the teacher of the causes of existence that I desired. I imagined he would tell me first whether the earth is flat or round, and whichever was true, he would go on to explain the cause and the necessity of its being so. Then he would teach me the nature of the best and show that this was best. If he said the earth was in the center, he would further explain that this position was the best, and I would be satisfied with the explanation and want no other sort of cause. I thought I would then go on and ask him about the sun, moon and stars, and that he would explain their comparative swiftness, their returnings and their various states, active and passive, and how all of them were for the best.

For I could not imagine that, when he spoke of mind as the disposer of them, he would give any account of their being as they are other than that this was best. I thought that when he had explained to me in detail the cause of each and the cause of all, he would go on to explain what was best for each and what was good for all. I would not have sold these hopes for a large sum of money. I seized the books and read them as fast as I could, in my eagerness to know the better and the worse.

What expectations I had formed, and how grievously I was disappointed! As I read on, I found my philosopher altogether abandoning mind and every other principle of order, and having recourse to air, ether, water and other oddities.

I might compare him to a person who began by maintaining that mind is the cause of the actions of Socrates, but who then tried to explain the causes of my several actions in detail. He would show that I sit here because my body is made up of bones and muscles. The bones, he would say, are hard and have joints that divide them, and the muscles are elastic and cover the bones, which are also enclosed by flesh and skin. And as the bones are lifted at their joints by the contraction or relaxation of the muscles, I am able to bend my limbs, and this is why I am sitting here in a curved posture. That is what he would say. He would have a similar explanation of my talking to you, which he would attribute to sound, air and hearing, and he would assign ten thousand other causes of the same sort. He would forget to mention the true cause, which is that the Athenians have thought fit to condemn me, and so I have thought it better and more right to stay here and undergo my sentence. For I am inclined to think that these muscles and bones of mine would have gone off long ago to Megara or Boeotia — by the dog they would — if they had been moved only by their own idea of what was best, and if I had not chosen the better and nobler part, instead of playing truant and running away, and endured whatever punishment the state inflicts. There is surely a strange confusion of causes and conditions in all this.

It may indeed be said that without bones and muscles and the other parts of the body I cannot carry out my purposes. But to say that I do what I do because of them, and that this is how mind acts, and not from the choice of the best, is a very careless and idle way of speaking. I wonder that they cannot distinguish the cause from the condition, which the many, feeling about in the dark, are always mistaking and misnaming. So one man makes a vortex all around the earth and steadies it by the heaven. Another gives the air as a support to the earth, which he treats as a sort of broad trough. It never enters their minds that any power which arranges things as they are arranges them for the best. Instead of finding any superior strength in that power, they expect to discover another Atlas of the world, stronger and more everlasting and more containing than the good. Of the obligatory and containing power of the good they think nothing. Yet this is the principle I would gladly learn, if anyone would teach me. But since I have failed, either by my own discovery or by learning from anyone else, to find the nature of the best, I will show you, if you like, what I have found to be the second best way of inquiring into the cause.
I should very much like to hear it, he replied.

Socrates went on: I thought that, since I had failed in the contemplation of true existence, I should take care not to lose the eye of my soul. People may injure their bodily eye by watching and gazing at the sun during an eclipse, unless they take the precaution of looking only at its image reflected in water or some similar medium. In the same way, I was afraid that my soul might be blinded altogether if I looked at things with my eyes or tried to grasp them with the help of the senses. So I thought I had better have recourse to the world of mind and look there for the truth of existence. I dare say the comparison is not perfect — for I am very far from admitting that he who contemplates existences through the medium of thought sees them only 'through a glass darkly,' any more than he who considers them in action and operation. However, this was the method I adopted. I first assumed some principle that I judged to be the strongest. Then I affirmed as true whatever seemed to agree with it, whether it concerned the cause or anything else, and I regarded whatever disagreed with it as untrue. But I should like to explain my meaning more clearly, since I do not think you understand me yet.
No indeed, replied Cebes, not very well.

There is nothing new, he said, in what I am about to tell you. It is only what I have always and everywhere been repeating, in the previous discussion and on other occasions. I want to show you the nature of the cause that has occupied my thoughts. I shall have to go back to those familiar words that are in everyone's mouth, and first assume that there is an absolute beauty and goodness and greatness, and the like. Grant me this, and I hope to be able to show you the nature of the cause and to prove the immortality of the soul.
Cebes said: You may go ahead with the proof at once, for I grant you this.

Well, he said, I should like to know whether you agree with me in the next step. For I cannot help thinking that if there is anything beautiful besides absolute beauty — should there be such a thing — it can be beautiful only insofar as it partakes of absolute beauty. And I should say the same of everything. Do you agree with this notion of the cause?
Yes, he said, I agree.

He went on: I know nothing and can understand nothing of those other wise causes that are alleged. If a person tells me that the bloom of color, or shape, or any such thing is a source of beauty, I leave all that aside, since it only confuses me. Simply and singly, and perhaps foolishly, I hold and am assured in my own mind that nothing makes a thing beautiful except the presence and participation of beauty, however or in whatever way it is obtained. As to the way, I am uncertain; but I stoutly contend that by beauty all beautiful things become beautiful. This seems to me the safest answer I can give, to myself or to another. I cling to it, persuaded that this principle will never be overthrown, and that to myself or to anyone who asks, I may safely reply that by beauty beautiful things become beautiful. Do you not agree with me?
I do.
And that by greatness only great things become great, and greater things greater, and by smallness the less become less?
True.

Then suppose a person remarked that A is taller by a head than B, and B shorter by a head than A. You would refuse to admit his statement. You would stoutly contend that what you mean is only that the greater is greater by, and by reason of, greatness, and the less is less only by, and by reason of, smallness. In this way you would avoid the danger of saying that the greater is greater and the less less by the measure of the head, which is the same in both. You would also avoid the monstrous absurdity of supposing that the greater man is greater by reason of the head, which is small. You would be afraid to draw such an inference, would you not?
Indeed, I should, said Cebes, laughing.

In the same way you would be afraid to say that ten exceeded eight by, and by reason of, two. You would say it was by, and by reason of, number. Or you would say that two cubits exceed one cubit not by a half, but by magnitude? For there is the same liability to error in all these cases.
Very true, he said.

Again, would you not be cautious about affirming that the addition of one to one, or the division of one, is the cause of two? You would loudly assert that you know of no way in which anything comes into existence except by participation in its own proper essence. So, as far as you know, the only cause of two is participation in duality — this is the way to make two — and participation in one is the way to make one. You would say: I will leave aside the puzzles of division and addition; wiser heads than mine may answer them. Inexperienced as I am, and ready, as the proverb says, to start at my own shadow, I cannot afford to give up the sure ground of a principle. And if anyone attacks you there, you would pay him no attention and give him no answer until you had seen whether the consequences that follow agree with one another or not. When you were then required to give an explanation of the principle itself, you would assume a higher principle, and then a higher, until you reached a resting place in the best of the higher ones. But you would not confuse the principle with its consequences in your reasoning, as the Eristics do — at least if you wanted to discover real existence. Not that this confusion matters to them, since they never care or think about the matter at all. They are clever enough to be well pleased with themselves, however great the turmoil of their ideas. But you, if you are a philosopher, will certainly do as I say.
What you say is most true, said Simmias and Cebes, both speaking at once.
ECHECRATES: Yes, Phaedo, and I do not wonder that they assented. Anyone with the least sense will acknowledge the wonderful clearness of Socrates' reasoning.
PHAEDO: Certainly, Echecrates, and that was the feeling of the whole company at the time.
ECHECRATES: Yes, and it is equally our feeling, who were not of the company and are now listening to your account. But what followed?
PHAEDO: After all this had been admitted, and they had agreed that ideas exist and that other things participate in them and take their names from them, Socrates, if I remember rightly, said —
This is your way of speaking. And yet when you say that Simmias is greater than Socrates and less than Phaedo, do you not say of Simmias that he has both greatness and smallness?
Yes, I do.

But you still allow that Simmias does not really exceed Socrates, as the words may seem to imply, because he is Simmias, but by reason of the size he has, and that Simmias does not exceed Socrates because he is Simmias, any more than because Socrates is Socrates, but because Socrates has smallness when compared with the greatness of Simmias?
True.
And if Phaedo exceeds him in size, this is not because Phaedo is Phaedo, but because Phaedo has greatness relative to Simmias, who is comparatively smaller?
That is true.

And therefore Simmias is said to be great, and is also said to be small, because he stands in a mean between them. He exceeds the smallness of the one by his greatness, and allows the greatness of the other to exceed his smallness. He added, laughing: I am speaking like a book, but I believe that what I am saying is true.
Simmias assented.

I speak as I do because I want you to agree with me in thinking not only that absolute greatness will never be both great and small, but also that greatness in us, or in the concrete, will never admit the small or admit of being exceeded. Instead, one of two things will happen. Either the greater will flee or retire before its opposite, the less, or it will already have ceased to exist at the approach of the less. But it will not be changed by allowing or admitting smallness. Even I, having received and admitted smallness when compared with Simmias, remain just as I was, and am the same small person. And as the idea of greatness can never condescend to be or become small, in the same way the smallness in us cannot be or become great. Nor can any other opposite that remains the same ever be or become its own opposite. It either passes away or perishes in the change.
That, replied Cebes, is quite my notion.

At this one of the company, though I do not exactly remember which of them, said: In heaven's name, is this not the direct contrary of what was admitted before — that the less came out of the greater and the greater out of the less, and that opposites were simply generated from opposites? But now this principle seems to be utterly denied.

Socrates inclined his head toward the speaker and listened. I like your courage, he said, in reminding us of this. But you do not observe that the two cases differ. Then we were speaking of opposites in the concrete; now we are speaking of the essential opposite, which, as is affirmed, can never be at variance with itself, either in us or in nature. Then, my friend, we were speaking of things in which opposites are inherent and which are named after them. Now we are speaking of the opposites that are inherent in those things and that give them their names. And these essential opposites will never, as we maintain, admit of generation into or out of one another. At the same time he turned to Cebes and said: Are you at all disconcerted, Cebes, by our friend's objection?
No, I do not feel disconcerted, said Cebes; and yet I cannot deny that objections often disturb me.
Then we are agreed after all, said Socrates, that an opposite will never in any case be opposed to itself?
To that we are quite agreed, he replied.
Once more, let me ask you to consider the question from another point of view and see whether you agree with me. There is a thing you call heat, and another thing you call cold?
Certainly.
But are they the same as fire and snow?
Most assuredly not.
Heat is a thing different from fire, and cold is not the same as snow?
Yes.

And yet you will surely admit that when snow, as was said before, is under the influence of heat, they will not remain snow and heat; but at the advance of the heat, the snow will either retire or perish?
Very true, he replied.
And the fire too, at the advance of the cold, will either retire or perish. When the fire is under the influence of the cold, they will not remain as before, fire and cold.
That is true, he said.

And in some cases the name of the idea is attached to the idea in an eternal connection, and anything else that is not the idea but exists only in the form of the idea may also lay claim to the name. I will try to make this clearer with an example. The odd number is always called by the name of odd?
Very true.

But is this the only thing called odd? Are there not other things that have their own name and yet are called odd, because, although they are not the same as oddness, they are never without oddness? That is what I mean to ask. Do numbers such as three not belong to the class of the odd? There are many other examples. Would you not say that three may be called by its proper name and also be called odd, which is not the same as three? And this may be said not only of three but also of five, and of every alternate number. Each of them is odd without being oddness. In the same way two and four, and the rest of the series of alternate numbers, are each even without being evenness. Do you agree?
Of course.

Then mark the point I am aiming at. Not only do essential opposites exclude one another, but so do concrete things that are not in themselves opposed and yet contain opposites. These, I say, likewise reject the idea that is opposed to the one contained in them, and when it approaches they either perish or withdraw. For example, will the number three not endure annihilation, or anything else, sooner than be turned into an even number while remaining three?
Very true, said Cebes.
And yet, he said, the number two is surely not opposed to the number three?
It is not.
Then not only do opposite ideas repel one another's advance, but there are also other natures that repel the approach of opposites.
Very true, he said.
Suppose, he said, that we try, if possible, to determine what these are.
By all means.
Are they not, Cebes, the things that compel whatever they possess to take not only their own form but also the form of some opposite?
What do you mean?
I mean what I was just saying, and what I am sure you know: the things that the number three possesses must be not only three in number but also odd.
Quite true.
And the opposite idea will never intrude on this oddness, of which the number three has the impress?
No.
And this impress was given by the odd principle?
Yes.
And the even is opposed to the odd?
True.
So the idea of the even number will never come to three?
No.
Then three has no part in the even?
None.
Then the triad, or number three, is uneven?
Very true.

To return, then, to my distinction of natures that are not opposed and yet do not admit opposites. In the instance given, three is not opposed to the even, yet it does not for that reason admit the even, but always brings the opposite into play on the other side. Likewise two does not receive the odd, nor fire the cold. From these examples (and there are many more) perhaps you can reach the general conclusion that not only will opposites not receive opposites, but nothing that brings an opposite will admit the opposite of what it brings, in that to which it brings it. Let me recapitulate, for there is no harm in repetition. The number five will not admit the nature of the even, any more than ten, the double of five, will admit the nature of the odd. The double has another opposite and is not strictly opposed to the odd, but it nevertheless rejects the odd altogether. Nor will parts in the ratio 3:2, nor any fraction containing a half, nor any containing a third, admit the notion of the whole, although they are not opposed to the whole. You will agree?
Yes, he said, I agree entirely and follow you in that.

And now, he said, let us begin again. Do not answer my question in the words in which I ask it. Give me not the old safe answer I spoke of at first, but another equally safe, whose truth you will infer from what has just been said. I mean this. If anyone asks you what it is whose presence in the body makes it hot, you will reply not heat (this is what I call the safe and stupid answer) but fire, a far better answer, which we are now in a position to give. Or if anyone asks you why a body is diseased, you will not say from disease but from fever. And instead of saying that oddness is the cause of odd numbers, you will say that the monad is the cause of them. And so with things in general. I dare say you will understand well enough without my giving any further examples.
Yes, he said, I quite understand you.
Tell me, then, what is it whose presence will make the body alive?
The soul, he replied.
And is this always the case?
Yes, he said, of course.
Then whatever the soul possesses, to that it comes bearing life?
Yes, certainly.
And is there any opposite to life?
There is, he said.
And what is that?
Death.
Then the soul, as has been acknowledged, will never receive the opposite of what it brings.
Impossible, replied Cebes.
And now, he said, what did we just now call the principle that repels the even?
The odd.
And the principle that repels the musical, or the just?
The unmusical, he said, and the unjust.
And what do we call the principle that does not admit of death?
The immortal, he said.
And does the soul admit of death?
No.

chapters.title: The Soul Is Immortal
paragraphs: So the soul is immortal?
Yes, he said.
And can we say that this has been proven?
Yes, Socrates, he replied, it has been abundantly proven.
Suppose the odd were imperishable. Then wouldn't three have to be imperishable too?
Of course.

And suppose that which is cold were imperishable. When the warm principle came at the snow, wouldn't the snow have had to withdraw whole and unmelted? For it could never have perished, and it could never have stayed and let the heat in.
True, he said.
In the same way, if the uncooling or warm principle were imperishable, then when cold attacked the fire, the fire would not have perished or been put out, but would have gone away unaffected?
Certainly, he said.

And we can say the same of the immortal. If the immortal is also imperishable, then when death attacks the soul, the soul cannot perish. For the argument so far shows that the soul will not admit death and will never be dead, just as three, or the odd number, will not admit the even, and as fire, or the heat in the fire, will not admit the cold. Yet someone may say: 'Granted that the odd does not become even when the even approaches, why couldn't the odd perish and the even take its place?' To a man who objects in this way we cannot answer that the odd is imperishable, because that has not been agreed. If it had been agreed, we could easily maintain that when the even approached, the odd and the number three departed; and the same argument would hold for fire and heat and everything else.
Very true.

And the same goes for the immortal. If the immortal is also imperishable, then the soul will be imperishable as well as immortal. If it is not, we will need some other proof that the soul is imperishable.
No other proof is needed, he said. For if the immortal, which lasts forever, can perish, then nothing is imperishable.
Yes, replied Socrates, and yet everyone will agree that God, and the essential form of life, and the immortal in general, will never perish.
Yes, everyone, he said, that is true; and what is more, the gods too, if I am not mistaken, as well as men.
Since the immortal is indestructible, then, mustn't the soul, if it is immortal, also be imperishable?
Most certainly.
Then when death comes at a man, the mortal part of him may be supposed to die, but the immortal part withdraws as death approaches and is kept safe and sound?
True.
Then, Cebes, beyond question the soul is immortal and imperishable, and our souls will truly exist in another world!

I am convinced, Socrates, said Cebes, and I have no further objection. But if my friend Simmias, or anyone else, has something more to say, he had better speak out and not stay silent. I do not know what other occasion he can put it off to, if he wants to say something or hear something said.

But I have nothing more to say, replied Simmias, and after what has been said I can see no reason for doubt. Still, when I think of the greatness of the subject and the weakness of man, I feel uncertain in my own mind, and I cannot help it.

Yes, Simmias, replied Socrates, that is well said. And I may add that first principles, even if they seem certain, should be examined carefully. When they have been satisfactorily established, you may then, I think, follow the course of the argument with a kind of hesitating confidence in human reason; and if that course is plain and clear, there will be no need for further inquiry.
Very true.

But then, my friends, he said, if the soul is really immortal, what care it needs, not only for the stretch of time we call life, but for all eternity! And the danger of neglecting it, seen in this light, does appear to be terrible. If death were the end of everything, the wicked would have made a good bargain by dying, since they would be rid, along with their souls, not only of the body but of their own evil. But now that the soul is clearly immortal, there is no release or salvation from evil except to attain the highest virtue and wisdom. For when the soul goes on its journey to the world below, it takes nothing with it but its nurture and education; and these are said to bring the greatest benefit or the greatest harm to the dead person, right at the start of the journey there.

For they say that after death the genius that was assigned to each person in life leads him to a certain place. There the dead are gathered together, and after judgment has been given they pass into the world below, following the guide who is appointed to conduct them from this world to the other. When they have received their due there and stayed their time, another guide brings them back again after many long ages. Now the way to the other world is not, as Aeschylus says in the Telephus, a single straight path. If it were, no guide would be needed, since no one could miss it. But there are many forks and windings in the road, as I infer from the rites and sacrifices offered to the gods below at places where three ways meet on earth.

The wise and orderly soul follows the straight path and is aware of its surroundings. But the soul that desires the body, as I said before, has long fluttered around the lifeless body and the visible world. After many struggles and much suffering, it is carried off with difficulty and by force by its attendant genius. When it arrives at the place where the other souls are gathered, if it is impure and has done impure deeds, such as foul murders or other crimes akin to these, the works of brothers in crime, then everyone flees from that soul and turns away. No one will be its companion or its guide, and it wanders alone in utter misery until certain times are fulfilled. When they are fulfilled, it is carried irresistibly to the dwelling that fits it. In the same way every pure and just soul, which has passed through life in the company and under the guidance of the gods, has its own proper home.
Now the earth has many wonderful regions. In its nature and size it is very unlike what the geographers suppose, as I believe on the authority of someone I will not name.
What do you mean, Socrates? said Simmias. I have heard many descriptions of the earth myself, but I do not know which of them you believe, and I should very much like to know.

If I had the art of Glaucus, Simmias, replied Socrates, I would tell you, although I do not know that even the art of Glaucus could prove my tale true, and I could never prove it myself; and even if I could, Simmias, I fear my life would end before the argument was finished. I can, however, describe the shape of the earth and its regions as I conceive them.
That, said Simmias, will be enough.

Well, then, he said, I am convinced that the earth is a round body in the center of the heavens. So it needs no air or any similar force to support it. It is held in place, and kept from falling or tilting in any direction, by the even balance of the surrounding heaven and by its own equipoise. For a thing in equipoise at the center of something evenly spread around it will not tilt in any direction, even slightly, but will always remain in the same state and not deviate. That is my first notion.
And surely it is a correct one, said Simmias.

I also believe that the earth is very large, and that we who live in the region from the river Phasis to the Pillars of Heracles occupy only a small portion of it around the sea, like ants or frogs around a marsh. There are other people living in many other places like ours. For all over the face of the earth there are hollows of various shapes and sizes, into which the water and the mist and the lower air collect. But the true earth is pure and lies in the pure heaven, where the stars also are. This heaven is the one we commonly call the ether, and our own earth is its sediment, gathering in the hollows below. We who live in these hollows are deceived into thinking that we live above, on the surface of the earth. It is just as if a creature at the bottom of the sea imagined that he was on the surface of the water, and that the sea was the heaven through which he saw the sun and the other stars. Because of his weakness and sluggishness he has never come up to the surface, and has never lifted up his head and seen, or heard from anyone who had seen, how much purer and fairer the world above is than his own. Our case is exactly the same. We live in a hollow of the earth and imagine that we are on the surface; and we call the air the heaven, in which we imagine that the stars move.

But the fact is that, because of our weakness and sluggishness, we cannot reach the surface of the air. If a man could reach its outer limit, or take the wings of a bird and fly to the top, he would put his head up like a fish lifting its head out of the water to see this world, and he would see a world beyond. And if human nature could bear the sight, he would acknowledge that this other world is the place of the true heaven and the true light and the true earth. For our earth, and its stones, and the whole region around us, are spoiled and corroded, as everything in the sea is corroded by the brine. Nothing noble or perfect grows there, only caverns, and sand, and an endless slough of mud; and even the shore cannot be compared with the fairer sights of this world. Still less can this world be compared with the other. About that upper earth under the heaven, Simmias, I can tell you a charming tale that is well worth hearing.
And we, Socrates, replied Simmias, will be delighted to listen to you.

The tale, my friend, he said, is this. First of all, when the earth is looked at from above, it looks streaked, like one of those balls covered with twelve pieces of leather. It is decked with various colors, of which the colors painters use here are in a way samples. There the whole earth is made of such colors, and they are far brighter and clearer than ours. There is a purple of wonderful brilliance, and the radiance of gold, and the white in the earth is whiter than any chalk or snow. The earth is made up of these and other colors, more numerous and fairer than any the human eye has seen. Even the hollows I spoke of, filled with air and water, have a color of their own and are seen as light gleaming among the variety of the other colors, so that the whole presents a single, continuous appearance of variety in unity. In this fair region everything that grows, trees and flowers and fruits, is fairer in the same degree than anything here. And there are hills whose stones are smoother and more transparent, and fairer in color, in the same degree than our highly valued emeralds and sardonyxes and jaspers and other gems, which are only tiny fragments of them. For there all the stones are like our precious stones, and fairer still (compare Republic).

The reason is that they are pure. Unlike our precious stones, they are not infected or corroded by the corrupt, briny elements that coagulate among us and breed foulness and disease in earth and stones, as well as in animals and plants. They are the jewels of the upper earth, which also shines with gold and silver and the like. They lie set in the light of day, large and abundant and in all places, making the earth a sight to gladden the eye of the beholder. There are animals and men there too, some in a middle region, others living about the air as we live about the sea, and others on islands which the air flows around, near the mainland. In a word, they use the air as we use water and the sea, and the ether is to them what the air is to us. Moreover, the temperate climate of their seasons keeps them free from disease, and they live much longer than we do. Their sight and hearing and smell and all their other senses are far more perfect than ours, in the same proportion that air is purer than water or the ether than air. They also have temples and sacred places in which the gods really dwell, and they hear the gods' voices and receive their answers, and are aware of them and talk with them. They see the sun, moon, and stars as they truly are, and the rest of their blessedness is of a piece with this.

Such is the nature of the whole earth and of the things around it. All over the globe there are many regions in the hollows on its surface. Some are deeper and more extended than the one we live in, some are deeper but have a narrower opening than ours, and some are shallower and also wider. All of them have numerous perforations, and there are passages, broad and narrow, in the interior of the earth connecting them with one another. Into these and out of them, as into basins, flows a vast tide of water, along with huge underground streams of never-failing rivers, springs hot and cold, a great fire, great rivers of fire, and streams of liquid mud, thin or thick (like the rivers of mud in Sicily, and the lava streams that follow them). The regions the streams happen to flow through are filled up with them. And there is a swinging or see-saw in the interior of the earth which moves all this up and down, and it is due to the following cause. There is a chasm that is the vastest of them all and pierces right through the whole earth. This is the chasm Homer describes in these words:
'Far off, where is the inmost depth beneath the earth;'

He and many other poets have called it Tartarus in other places. The see-saw is caused by the streams flowing into and out of this chasm, and each stream has the nature of the soil it flows through. The streams are always flowing in and out because the watery element has no bed or bottom, but swings and surges up and down, and the surrounding wind and air do the same. They follow the water up and down, this way and that, over the earth, just as in breathing the air is always being drawn in and let out. The wind swinging in and out with the water produces fearful and irresistible blasts. When the waters rush back into the lower parts of the earth, as they are called, they flow through the earth in those regions and fill them up like water raised by a pump. When they leave those regions and rush back here, they fill the hollows here again, and when these are full they flow through underground channels and find their way to their several places, forming seas, and lakes, and rivers, and springs. From there they enter the earth again. Some make a long circuit through many lands, others go to a few places not so far away; and they fall into Tartarus again, some at a point a good deal lower than where they rose, others not much lower, but all in some degree lower than the point they came from.

Some burst out again on the opposite side, some on the same side, and some wind around the earth with one fold or many, like the coils of a serpent, and descend as far as they can, but always return and fall into the chasm. Rivers flowing in either direction can descend only to the center and no further, for on the far side of the center the rivers face a steep rise.

Now these rivers are many and mighty and of different kinds, and there are four principal ones. The greatest, and the outermost, is the one called Oceanus, which flows around the earth in a circle. In the opposite direction flows Acheron, which passes under the earth through desert places into the Acherusian lake. To the shores of this lake the souls of most of the dead go; and after waiting an appointed time, longer for some and shorter for others, they are sent back to be born again as animals. The third river passes out between the two, and near its outlet it pours into a vast region of fire and forms a lake larger than the Mediterranean Sea, boiling with water and mud. From there it goes on, muddy and turbid, winding around the earth, and comes, among other places, to the edges of the Acherusian Lake. It does not mingle with the waters of the lake, but after making many coils around the earth it plunges into Tartarus at a deeper level. This is the river called Pyriphlegethon, which throws up jets of fire in different parts of the earth.

The fourth river goes out on the opposite side and falls first into a wild and savage region, which is all dark blue in color, like lapis lazuli. This is the river called the Stygian river, and it falls into and forms the Lake Styx. After falling into the lake and receiving strange powers in its waters, it passes under the earth, winding around in the opposite direction, and comes near the Acherusian lake from the side opposite Pyriphlegethon. The water of this river too mingles with no other, but flows around in a circle and falls into Tartarus opposite Pyriphlegethon. The name of this river, as the poets say, is Cocytus.

Such is the nature of the other world. When the dead arrive at the place to which the genius of each leads them, they are first of all sentenced, according to whether they have lived well and piously or not. Those who seem to have lived neither well nor badly go to the river Acheron. They embark on whatever vessels they find and are carried in them to the lake. There they dwell and are purified of their evil deeds; and when they have suffered the penalty for the wrongs they have done to others, they are absolved, and each receives the rewards of his good deeds according to his deserts. But those who seem incurable because of the greatness of their crimes, who have committed many terrible acts of sacrilege, or foul and violent murders, or the like, are hurled into Tartarus, which is their fitting destiny, and they never come out.

Others have committed crimes which, although great, are not irremediable. For example, in a moment of anger they have done violence to a father or a mother and have repented for the rest of their lives, or they have taken another's life in similarly extenuating circumstances. These are plunged into Tartarus, and they must endure its pains for a year. At the end of the year the wave casts them out, mere homicides by way of Cocytus, parricides and matricides by Pyriphlegethon. They are carried to the Acherusian lake, and there they lift up their voices and call on the people they have killed or wronged, begging them to have pity and be kind, and to let them come out into the lake. If they prevail, they come out and their troubles cease. If not, they are carried back into Tartarus and from there into the rivers again, without end, until they obtain mercy from those they have wronged; for that is the sentence their judges have given them. And those who have been pre-eminent for holiness of life are released from this earthly prison and go to their pure home above, and live on the purer earth. Of these, the ones who have sufficiently purified themselves with philosophy live from then on altogether without the body, in dwellings fairer still, which cannot be described, and of which I do not have time to tell.
Seeing all this, then, Simmias, what should we not do to obtain virtue and wisdom in this life? The prize is fair, and the hope is great!

chapters.title: The Death of Socrates
paragraphs: A man of sense ought not to say, and I will not be very confident, that my description of the soul and its mansions is exactly true. But I do say that, since the soul has been shown to be immortal, he may venture to think, not improperly or unworthily, that something of the kind is true. The venture is a glorious one, and he ought to comfort himself with words like these, which is why I am lengthening out the tale. So I say, let a man be of good cheer about his soul if he has cast away the pleasures and ornaments of the body as alien to him and working harm rather than good, and has sought after the pleasures of knowledge. Such a man has arrayed the soul not in some foreign attire but in its own proper jewels, temperance and justice and courage and nobility and truth. Adorned in these, the soul is ready to go on its journey to the world below when its hour comes. You, Simmias and Cebes, and all other men, will depart at some time or other. Me, as the tragic poet would say, the voice of fate already calls. Soon I must drink the poison; and I think I had better go to the bath first, so that the women will not have the trouble of washing my body after I am dead.
When he had finished speaking, Crito said: 'And do you have any commands for us, Socrates? Is there anything you want to say about your children, or about any other matter in which we can serve you?'

Nothing particular, Crito, he replied. Only what I have always told you: take care of yourselves. That is a service you can always be doing for me and mine and for all of us, whether you promise to or not. But if you have no thought for yourselves, and do not care to walk by the rule I have laid down for you, now and not for the first time, then it will be of no use, however much you may profess or promise at the moment.
We will do our best, said Crito. And in what way shall we bury you?

He said, 'In any way you like; but you must get hold of me, and make sure that I do not run away from you.' Then he turned to us and added with a smile: 'I cannot make Crito believe that I am the same Socrates who has been talking and conducting the argument. He fancies that I am the other Socrates, whom he will soon see as a dead body, and he asks how he should bury me. I have spoken many words to show that when I have drunk the poison I shall leave you and go to the joys of the blessed. But these words of mine, with which I was comforting you and myself, have had no effect on Crito, as I can see. So I want you to be my surety to him now, as he was surety to the judges for me at the trial. But let the promise be of a different sort. He was surety to the judges that I would stay; you must be my surety to him that I shall not stay but go away and depart. Then he will suffer less at my death, and will not be grieved when he sees my body being burned or buried. I would not have him sorrow over my hard lot, or say at the burial, "Thus we lay out Socrates," or "Thus we follow him to the grave," or "Thus we bury him." For false words are not only evil in themselves, they also infect the soul with evil. Be of good cheer, then, my dear Crito, and say that you are burying my body only; and do with that whatever is usual, and whatever you think best.'

When he had said this, he got up and went into a room to bathe. Crito followed him and told us to wait. So we stayed behind, talking over what had been said and thinking about it, and also about the greatness of our sorrow. He was like a father we were about to lose, and we were going to spend the rest of our lives as orphans. After his bath his children were brought to him (he had two young sons and an older one), and the women of his family came as well. He talked to them and gave them a few directions in the presence of Crito. Then he sent them away and came back to us.

By now the hour of sunset was near, for a good deal of time had passed while he was inside. When he came out he sat down with us again after his bath, but not much was said. Soon the jailer, who was the servant of the Eleven, came in and stood beside him and said: 'Socrates, I know you to be the noblest and gentlest and best of all who have ever come to this place, and I will not hold against you the angry feelings of other men, who rage and swear at me when, in obedience to the authorities, I tell them to drink the poison. Indeed, I am sure you will not be angry with me; for others, as you know, and not I, are to blame. So farewell, and try to bear lightly what must be. You know my errand.' Then he burst into tears, turned away and went out.

Socrates looked at him and said: 'I return your good wishes, and I will do as you say.' Then he turned to us and said: 'How charming the man is! Ever since I have been in prison he has been coming to see me, and sometimes he would talk to me, and he was as good to me as could be; and now see how generously he sorrows on my account. We must do as he says, Crito. So let the cup be brought, if the poison is prepared; and if not, let the attendant prepare some.'

Yet, said Crito, the sun is still on the hilltops, and I know that many a man has taken the draught late. After the announcement has been made to him, he has eaten and drunk and enjoyed the company of those he loves. Do not hurry; there is time enough.

Socrates said: Yes, Crito, and the men you speak of are right to act so, for they think they will gain by the delay. But I am right not to follow their example, for I do not think I would gain anything by drinking the poison a little later. I should only be ridiculous in my own eyes for sparing and saving a life that is already forfeit. Please do as I say, then, and do not refuse me.

Crito made a sign to the servant who was standing by. He went out, and after being gone for some time he returned with the jailer, who was carrying the cup of poison. Socrates said: 'You, my good friend, who are experienced in these matters, must tell me how to proceed.' The man answered: 'You have only to walk about until your legs are heavy, and then lie down, and the poison will act.' At the same time he handed the cup to Socrates. He took it in the easiest and gentlest manner, Echecrates, without the least fear or change of color or expression, looking at the man with all his eyes, as was his way, and said: 'What do you say about pouring a libation from this cup to some god? May I, or not?' The man answered: 'We prepare only as much as we think enough, Socrates.' 'I understand,' he said, 'but I may and must pray to the gods that my journey from this world to the other prosper. So I pray, and so be it according to my prayer.' Then he raised the cup to his lips and, quite readily and cheerfully, drank off the poison. Until then most of us had been able to control our sorrow; but now that we saw him drinking, and saw that he had finished the draught, we could no longer hold back. In spite of myself my own tears were flowing fast, so that I covered my face and wept, not for him, but at the thought of my own calamity in having to part from such a friend.

I was not the first. Crito, when he found he could not restrain his tears, had got up, and I followed. At that moment Apollodorus, who had been weeping all the time, broke out in a loud and passionate cry that made cowards of us all. Socrates alone kept his calm. 'What is this strange outcry?' he said. 'I sent away the women mainly so that they would not behave in this way, for I have been told that a man should die in peace. Be quiet, then, and have patience.' When we heard his words we were ashamed and held back our tears. He walked about until, as he said, his legs began to fail, and then he lay on his back, as he had been told. The man who had given him the poison looked at his feet and legs from time to time. After a while he pressed his foot hard and asked if he could feel it; and Socrates said no. Then he pressed his leg, and so on upwards and upwards, and showed us that he was cold and stiff. Socrates felt them himself and said: 'When the poison reaches the heart, that will be the end.' He was beginning to grow cold about the groin when he uncovered his face, for he had covered himself up, and said, and these were his last words: 'Crito, I owe a rooster to Asclepius; will you remember to pay the debt?' 'The debt shall be paid,' said Crito; 'is there anything else?' There was no answer to this question; but in a minute or two a movement was heard, and the attendants uncovered him. His eyes were set, and Crito closed his eyes and mouth.
Such was the end, Echecrates, of our friend. Of all the men of his time whom I have known, I may truly say that he was the wisest and justest and best.
